source_records.title: Discounting timing strategies
source_records.abstract: A variety of timing strategies shown to generate alpha and high Sharpe ratios at the monthly horizon exhibit substantially deteriorated performance at longer investment horizons. The effect is large: multi-factor alphas are more than halved going from one-month to 10-year returns, and factors that exploit time-series predictability drive them to zero. I argue that such return dynamics reflect compensation for exposure to shocks that are particularly risky from a long-horizon investor’s perspective. I illustrate the idea by showing that seasonality in the volatility of price-of-risk and expected-cash-flow shocks generates seemingly profitable timing strategies.

A variety of timing strategies shown to generate alpha and high Sharpe ratios at the monthly horizon exhibit substantially deteriorated performance at longer investment horizons. The effect is large: multi-factor alphas are more than halved going from one-month to 10-year returns, and factors that exploit time-series predictability drive them to zero. I argue that such return dynamics reflect compensation for exposure to shocks that are particularly risky from a long-horizon investor’s perspective. I illustrate the idea by showing that seasonality in the volatility of price-of-risk and expected-cash-flow shocks generates seemingly profitable timing strategies.

The effect is large: multi-factor alphas are more than halved going from one-month to 10-year returns, and factors that exploit time-series predictability drive them to zero. I argue that such return dynamics reflect compensation for exposure to shocks that are particularly risky from a long-horizon investor’s perspective. I illustrate the idea by showing that seasonality in the volatility of price-of-risk and expected-cash-flow shocks generates seemingly profitable timing strategies.

entries.title: Machine-learning about ESG preferences: Evidence from fund flows

source_records.title: Machine-learning about ESG preferences: Evidence from fund flows
source_records.abstract: We construct Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) scores for U.S. active equity mutual funds using roughly 500 metrics across ESG issues and rating agencies. Under a revealed-preference framework, we use machine learning to identify issues driving fund flows and generate ESG-driven flows as proxies for ESG performance. We estimate expected benchmark-adjusted returns using ex-post realized returns and ex-ante measures. Better-ESG funds attract larger subsequent flows and face fewer redemptions after poor performance, yet have lower expected returns, indicating flows reflect investor ESG preferences rather than high-return beliefs. Investors effectively pay $48 million more annually for a top-ESG fund.

Investors effectively pay $48 million more annually for a top-ESG fund.KeywordsESG; Fund flow; Value-added; Machine learningPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionAs investors allocate their savings in consideration of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors, it is important to know which ESG issues matter for investors, and how investors judge good versus bad ESG performance. Regulators, for example, need to know which ESG-related risks to highlight when proposing new disclosure rules.1 Practitioners and asset managers, meanwhile, have a business interest in understanding which ESG products are likely to be rated highly by investors.2 Accurate measures of ESG performance are also key to identifying ESG-return tradeoffs—i.e., whether products with better ESG characteristics tend to underperform in a financial sense. Yet, these questions are difficult to answer because investors’ ESG preferences are complex and likely focus on a specific few of many possible ESG issues. Indeed, Starks (2023) suggests that it does not make sense to talk about ESG issues as if they represent a consolidation of similar issues given the wide variety of designated ESG financial products.3 Furthermore, Berg et al. (2022a) find that ESG ratings services often disagree about a firm’s ESG performance. Such “ESG confusion” makes it difficult to objectively measure ESG performance even if one knew which issues were key to investors.In this paper, we use the capital flows of mutual funds to infer investors’ ESG preferences from their actions. Specifically, we relate flows to funds’ ESG scores covering a wide range of issues and rating agencies. This “revealed preference” approach identifies relevant scores based on their ability to forecast future flows.4 ESG scores plausibly contain relevant information because they are directly observed by many investors and may be correlated with latent variables that drive investor flows, such as ESG-related news events on media outlets and posts on social media about the fund or its top holdings.5 Our approach also yields accurate flow forecasts—“ESG-driven flow”—that concentrate the investor-relevant information in all scores. We propose that ESG-driven flow is a valid proxy for a fund’s ESG performance: funds with greater ESG-driven flow have ESG scores that are historically strong predictors of flows and, in this sense, align closely with investors’ preferences and have better ESG performance.Our analysis covers active equity mutual funds in the United States from 2011 to 2020. We construct a broad set of ESG scores for each fund using its stock holdings and stock-level ESG scores. These scores are based on about 500 underlying ESG metrics covering a wide range of ESG issues and six rating agencies—Sustainalytics, MSCI IVA, MSCI KLD, Refinitiv Asset4, RepRisk, and S&P Global. We categorize these metrics into a tractable number of 17 ESG issues so that, for example, all metrics related to carbon emissions and climate change are categorized into a single Climate Change & Emissions issue. In addition, we construct up to six rating agency-specific scores for each ESG issue, yielding a total of 91 scores across issues and rating agencies.6We first examine the predictive power of ESG scores for fund flows. We sort funds in month t−1 into deciles based on their scores and compute their average value-weighted flows over month t. Our first test uses a fund’s single composite ESG score obtained by averaging its 91 scores across all issues and rating agencies. Funds with scores in the top decile garner higher flows than bottom decile funds, with a flow spread of 5.36% (t-statistic =4.27).Next, we focus on scores for specific ESG issues, obtained by averaging scores across rating agencies. Many issues are associated with positive and significant flow spreads, including Waste & Pollution (E), Product Responsibility (S), and Business Ethics (G); in contrast, for other issues, the flow spreads are small and not significant. The observed heterogeneity in predictive power for investor capital flows across ESG issues supports the conjecture of Starks (2023) that, “...many, perhaps most, value and values investors do not employ the combined ESG score but rather are more interested in the individual components such as carbon footprint, animal rights, or governance quality.”We then exploit the heterogeneity in ESG scores across rating agencies. We first show that fund-level ESG scores inherit the well-known dispersion in ESG scores at the stock-level (Berg et al., 2022b). Specifically, the average pairwise correlation between rating agencies’ scores is just 0.17. The strength of the flow-ESG sensitivity is rating agency-specific for some issues but not others. For example, in case of Climate Change & Emissions, only the scores provided by Sustainalytics and RepRisk deliver positive and significant flow spreads while the Accounting & Transparency scores of nearly all rating agencies generate a significant flow response. Hence, relevant information about ESG performance is widespread across issues and rating agencies and, for some particular issues, investors respond to scores from any rating agency.To effectively capture the diverse ESG preferences driving investor capital allocation decisions, we adopt machine learning (ML) to generate accurate flow forecasts (“ESG-driven flows”) that incorporate the predictive power of all 91 ESG scores. Specifically, we use Boosted Regression Trees (BRT) as our baseline ML model to estimate the functional form relating scores available at month t−1 to flows in month t over a training and validation sample.7 We recursively train and validate BRT at each quarter-end using an expanding window of flows and scores. We then apply the trained model to generate monthly flow forecasts in the next quarter. This yields a panel of flow forecasts for each month and fund, denoted FlowESĜ, that avoids forward-looking information. By design, ESG-driven flows are higher for funds with ESG scores that are informative of future flows. In this sense, such funds align closely with investors’ ESG preferences and have better ESG performance.If FlowESĜ is a valid proxy for a fund’s ESG performance, then it should predict higher flows in the future. Indeed, we find that FlowESĜ in month t−1 predicts month-t flows outside of our training samples. Funds in the top decile of FlowESĜ realize annualized value-weighted flows of 8.86% (t-statistic =4.74) over the following month while those in the bottom decile realize −15.25% (t-statistic =−16.18). The difference, 24.11% (t-statistic =12.70), is four times larger than that from sorting on the simple composite ESG score and even more on any single score. Interestingly, the positive flows in the top decile group contrast with the overall pattern of negative flows among active equity mutual funds during the 2011–2020 period.FlowESĜ is novel because its predictive power is not subsumed by well-documented predictors of fund flows, including CAPM alpha (Barber et al., 2016), Morningstar Star Rating (Ben-David et al., 2022), and Morningstar Globe Rating (Hartzmark and Sussman, 2019). It is economically important: a one-standard-deviation increase in FlowESĜ produces 1.82% higher annualized flows, while one-standard-deviation increases in CAPM alpha and the Morningstar Star Rating are associated with higher flows of 3.00% and 2.52%, respectively. FlowESĜ also substantially outperforms simpler measures of ESG-driven flows, including those based on linear models and a narrower set of ESG scores. These empirical facts establish that combining ML with a broad set of ESG scores adds significant value in uncovering the relationship between fund flows and ESG scores.Three additional findings validate FlowESĜ as a proxy for a fund’s ESG performance. First, fund flows are more predictable when using only environmental scores (i.e., FlowÊ) following the adoption of the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, a high-profile international treaty aimed at addressing climate change. This is consistent with investors responding more favorably to better environmental performance when awareness of climate concerns is higher.8 By contrast, predictability based only on social (FlowŜ) and governance (FlowĜ) scores is not significantly altered over this period. Second, FlowESĜ performs better when it is estimated using the ESG scores of stocks in a fund’s top-dollar positions, rather than its middle- and bottom-dollar positions, consistent with investors reacting more strongly to salient information reflected in a fund’s top holdings. Third, FlowESĜ is more informative for funds with an explicit ESG mandate, suggesting that investors in such funds are more socially conscious and more sensitive to fund ESG performance.A natural and crucial question is whether FlowESĜ is also predictive of a fund’s financial performance. Asset managers often claim that they can boost portfolio returns by tilting toward sustainable assets, while a common theoretical view is that the benefits of ESG investing should be offset by lower expected returns as investors bid up the prices of assets with better ESG characteristics.9 To address this question, we extend the conceptual framework of Berk and Green (2004) to an ESG setting in which fund investors derive utility from both benchmark-adjusted returns (i.e., alpha) and non-pecuniary benefits from ESG investing (i.e., ESG performance). Funds face decreasing returns to scale in active portfolio management, and investors supply capital until the total value added from net-of-fees alpha and ESG performance is expected to be zero. The framework delivers two predictions. First, funds with higher alpha and ESG performance have higher future flows, consistent with our empirical evidence discussed above. Second, a fund’s value added from alpha—net-of-fees benchmark-adjusted returns multiplied by AUM—represents the shadow price of ESG performance, or equivalently the negative of ESG value added. In other words, a fund’s ESG performance is negatively associated with its financial value added and, hence, fund investors face an ESG–return trade-off.To test this prediction, we first compare the realized benchmark-adjusted returns of funds in the top decile of FlowESĜ with those in the bottom decile. The annualized average return spread over the subsequent 36 months is −0.72% (t-statistic =−2.48). The negative return predictability of FlowESĜ remains economically and statistically significant after controlling for fund characteristics, including fund size, expense ratio, turnover ratio, CAPM α, Morningstar Star Rating, and fund R2, a well-known predictor of fund performance (Amihud and Goyenko, 2013). Following the approach in Berk and Van Binsbergen (2015), we then compute funds’ value added and find that funds in the top decile of ESG performance deliver $48 million per year more ESG value added than funds in the bottom decile. Based on ex post realized fund returns, our findings suggest that mutual fund investors face an ESG–return tradeoff: funds with better ESG performance deliver significantly less value added from alpha.We also address the concern that ESG premia and value added may be estimated imprecisely because the time series of realized returns are short and noisy. At the stock level, prior studies address this issue by computing forward-looking, ex ante measures of expected returns (e.g., Pástor et al., 2022, Eskildsen et al., 2024). We apply this approach in the mutual fund setting to construct four ex ante measures of expected benchmark-adjusted fund returns and value added. These measures are based on alternative estimates of the expected returns of the stocks held by each fund and its benchmark index. Consistent with our results using ex post realized fund returns, high-FlowESĜ funds deliver lower expected benchmark-adjusted returns and higher expected ESG value added. In addition, the estimated ex ante return spreads have smaller standard errors and range from −0.38% to −2.34%, depending on the measure.Taken together, our evidence shows that investors respond positively to funds with better ESG performance (i.e., higher FlowESĜ), despite holding ex ante beliefs that such funds deliver poor financial performance. Hence, investors’ positive flow response to FlowESĜ likely reflects ESG preferences rather than the belief that a fund’s ESG tilts signal higher future returns. To further disentangle preferences from beliefs, we examine outflows (redemptions) from funds with better ESG performance when those funds perform poorly in returns (i.e., have a Morningstar Star Rating of one). Interestingly, we find that investors redeem less capital from such funds. This pattern is consistent with strong ESG preferences: investors continue to invest sustainably even when such funds perform poorly.Our main findings survive many variations of the baseline analysis. First, the predictive power of FlowESĜ is not materially altered by including FlowFundChar̂ and FlowPortChar̂—ML flow forecasts based on large sets of fund characteristics and portfolio characteristics constructed from firm financial ratios other than ESG scores. Second, our portfolio-sort results are qualitatively similar when using equally weighted portfolios instead of value-weighted portfolios, but the estimated dollar amount investors are willing to pay for a top ESG fund is smaller ($21 versus $48 million per year). Third, FlowESĜ remains predictive of future fund flows when it is constructed using alternative ML models—Elastic Net, Random Forest, and Convolutional Neural Networks—instead of BRT. Fourth, our qualitative results are unchanged when we regenerate FlowESĜ after excluding all scores from any given ESG rating agency, alleviating concerns that our findings are driven by any specific agency’s data. Finally, FlowESĜ has no predictive power in a placebo test in which it is generated by training on randomly reshuffled ESG scores, making it unlikely that our results are “hard-wired” into the ML methods.Our paper contributes to recent studies of ESG investing in the mutual fund space. While Hartzmark and Sussman (2019) find that mutual fund investors react favorably to Morningstar Globe Ratings after their introduction in 2016, Gantchev et al. (2024) find that Globe Ratings do not predict flows in more recent periods. Consistent with Gantchev et al. (2024), we find that Globe Ratings fail to predict flows over 2018–2020, a period far removed from their introduction. We introduce a novel measure of a fund’s ESG performance, FlowESĜ, based on the historical relation between investor capital flows and ESG scores. In contrast to Globe Ratings, FlowESĜ robustly predicts flows throughout our sample period.We contribute to the literature that separates preferences from beliefs. Gantchev et al. (2024) argue that mutual fund investors mainly care about return performance since Globe Ratings neither predict better returns nor generate a positive flow response. In contrast, we find that investors respond favorably to funds with higher FlowESĜ despite lower ex ante expected returns. Moreover, investors in funds with higher FlowESĜ are less likely to exit after poor return performance. These patterns suggest that investors are willing to sacrifice returns for better ESG performance as measured by FlowESĜ, supporting the notion that investors are driven by ESG preferences (e.g., Riedl and Smeets, 2017).10We also contribute to recent evidence on the ESG premium. Baker et al. (2022) find that investors are willing to pay 20 basis points per year more to invest in an index fund with an ESG mandate than in one without. We focus on active equity mutual funds rather than passive funds with an ESG mandate. Using a new proxy for a fund’s ESG performance, FlowESĜ, we show that the presence of an ESG mandate does not imply better ESG performance. In addition, according to our measure, a top-ESG-performing fund delivers a 0.72% lower net alpha and $48 million per year in higher ESG value added relative to a bottom-ESG fund. This magnitude is comparable to the value added of active mutual fund managers with top stock-selection skill (Berk and Van Binsbergen, 2015).Finally, we contribute to recent evidence that ESG scores can be misleading measures of actual ESG performance.11 We introduce FlowESĜ, a novel measure that better aligns fund-level ESG performance with revealed investor preferences. We show that funds with higher ESG-driven flows have lower ex ante expected returns, consistent with a competitive model in the spirit of Berk and Green (2004) extended to fund investors with ESG preferences. proposed.title: Machine-learning about ESG preferences: Evidence from fund flows
proposed.abstract: We construct Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) scores for U.S. active equity mutual funds using roughly 500 metrics across ESG issues and rating agencies. Under a revealed-preference framework, we use machine learning to identify issues driving fund flows and generate ESG-driven flows as proxies for ESG performance. We estimate expected benchmark-adjusted returns using ex-post realized returns and ex-ante measures. Better-ESG funds attract larger subsequent flows and face fewer redemptions after poor performance, yet have lower expected returns, indicating flows reflect investor ESG preferences rather than high-return beliefs. Investors effectively pay $48 million more annually for a top-ESG fund.

Regulators, for example, need to know which ESG-related risks to highlight when proposing new disclosure rules.1 Practitioners and asset managers, meanwhile, have a business interest in understanding which ESG products are likely to be rated highly by investors.2 Accurate measures of ESG performance are also key to identifying ESG-return tradeoffs—i.e., whether products with better ESG characteristics tend to underperform in a financial sense. Yet, these questions are difficult to answer because investors’ ESG preferences are complex and likely focus on a specific few of many possible ESG issues. Indeed, Starks (2023) suggests that it does not make sense to talk about ESG issues as if they represent a consolidation of similar issues given the wide variety of designated ESG financial products.3 Furthermore, Berg et al. (2022a) find that ESG ratings services often disagree about a firm’s ESG performance. Such “ESG confusion” makes it difficult to objectively measure ESG performance even if one knew which issues were key to investors.In this paper, we use the capital flows of mutual funds to infer investors’ ESG preferences from their actions. Specifically, we relate flows to funds’ ESG scores covering a wide range of issues and rating agencies. This “revealed preference” approach identifies relevant scores based on their ability to forecast future flows.4 ESG scores plausibly contain relevant information because they are directly observed by many investors and may be correlated with latent variables that drive investor flows, such as ESG-related news events on media outlets and posts on social media about the fund or its top holdings.5 Our approach also yields accurate flow forecasts—“ESG-driven flow”—that concentrate the investor-relevant information in all scores. We propose that ESG-driven flow is a valid proxy for a fund’s ESG performance: funds with greater ESG-driven flow have ESG scores that are historically strong predictors of flows and, in this sense, align closely with investors’ preferences and have better ESG performance.Our analysis covers active equity mutual funds in the United States from 2011 to 2020. We construct a broad set of ESG scores for each fund using its stock holdings and stock-level ESG scores. These scores are based on about 500 underlying ESG metrics covering a wide range of ESG issues and six rating agencies—Sustainalytics, MSCI IVA, MSCI KLD, Refinitiv Asset4, RepRisk, and S&P Global. We categorize these metrics into a tractable number of 17 ESG issues so that, for example, all metrics related to carbon emissions and climate change are categorized into a single Climate Change & Emissions issue. In addition, we construct up to six rating agency-specific scores for each ESG issue, yielding a total of 91 scores across issues and rating agencies.6We first examine the predictive power of ESG scores for fund flows. We sort funds in month t−1 into deciles based on their scores and compute their average value-weighted flows over month t. Our first test uses a fund’s single composite ESG score obtained by averaging its 91 scores across all issues and rating agencies. Funds with scores in the top decile garner higher flows than bottom decile funds, with a flow spread of 5.36% (t-statistic =4.27).Next, we focus on scores for specific ESG issues, obtained by averaging scores across rating agencies. Many issues are associated with positive and significant flow spreads, including Waste & Pollution (E), Product Responsibility (S), and Business Ethics (G); in contrast, for other issues, the flow spreads are small and not significant. The observed heterogeneity in predictive power for investor capital flows across ESG issues supports the conjecture of Starks (2023) that, “...many, perhaps most, value and values investors do not employ the combined ESG score but rather are more interested in the individual components such as carbon footprint, animal rights, or governance quality.”We then exploit the heterogeneity in ESG scores across rating agencies. We first show that fund-level ESG scores inherit the well-known dispersion in ESG scores at the stock-level (Berg et al., 2022b). Specifically, the average pairwise correlation between rating agencies’ scores is just 0.17. The strength of the flow-ESG sensitivity is rating agency-specific for some issues but not others. For example, in case of Climate Change & Emissions, only the scores provided by Sustainalytics and RepRisk deliver positive and significant flow spreads while the Accounting & Transparency scores of nearly all rating agencies generate a significant flow response. Hence, relevant information about ESG performance is widespread across issues and rating agencies and, for some particular issues, investors respond to scores from any rating agency.To effectively capture the diverse ESG preferences driving investor capital allocation decisions, we adopt machine learning (ML) to generate accurate flow forecasts (“ESG-driven flows”) that incorporate the predictive power of all 91 ESG scores. Specifically, we use Boosted Regression Trees (BRT) as our baseline ML model to estimate the functional form relating scores available at month t−1 to flows in month t over a training and validation sample.7 We recursively train and validate BRT at each quarter-end using an expanding window of flows and scores. We then apply the trained model to generate monthly flow forecasts in the next quarter. This yields a panel of flow forecasts for each month and fund, denoted FlowESĜ, that avoids forward-looking information. By design, ESG-driven flows are higher for funds with ESG scores that are informative of future flows. In this sense, such funds align closely with investors’ ESG preferences and have better ESG performance.If FlowESĜ is a valid proxy for a fund’s ESG performance, then it should predict higher flows in the future. Indeed, we find that FlowESĜ in month t−1 predicts month-t flows outside of our training samples. Funds in the top decile of FlowESĜ realize annualized value-weighted flows of 8.86% (t-statistic =4.74) over the following month while those in the bottom decile realize −15.25% (t-statistic =−16.18). The difference, 24.11% (t-statistic =12.70), is four times larger than that from sorting on the simple composite ESG score and even more on any single score. Interestingly, the positive flows in the top decile group contrast with the overall pattern of negative flows among active equity mutual funds during the 2011–2020 period.FlowESĜ is novel because its predictive power is not subsumed by well-documented predictors of fund flows, including CAPM alpha (Barber et al., 2016), Morningstar Star Rating (Ben-David et al., 2022), and Morningstar Globe Rating (Hartzmark and Sussman, 2019). It is economically important: a one-standard-deviation increase in FlowESĜ produces 1.82% higher annualized flows, while one-standard-deviation increases in CAPM alpha and the Morningstar Star Rating are associated with higher flows of 3.00% and 2.52%, respectively. FlowESĜ also substantially outperforms simpler measures of ESG-driven flows, including those based on linear models and a narrower set of ESG scores. These empirical facts establish that combining ML with a broad set of ESG scores adds significant value in uncovering the relationship between fund flows and ESG scores.Three additional findings validate FlowESĜ as a proxy for a fund’s ESG performance. First, fund flows are more predictable when using only environmental scores (i.e., FlowÊ) following the adoption of the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, a high-profile international treaty aimed at addressing climate change. This is consistent with investors responding more favorably to better environmental performance when awareness of climate concerns is higher.8 By contrast, predictability based only on social (FlowŜ) and governance (FlowĜ) scores is not significantly altered over this period. Second, FlowESĜ performs better when it is estimated using the ESG scores of stocks in a fund’s top-dollar positions, rather than its middle- and bottom-dollar positions, consistent with investors reacting more strongly to salient information reflected in a fund’s top holdings. Third, FlowESĜ is more informative for funds with an explicit ESG mandate, suggesting that investors in such funds are more socially conscious and more sensitive to fund ESG performance.A natural and crucial question is whether FlowESĜ is also predictive of a fund’s financial performance. Asset managers often claim that they can boost portfolio returns by tilting toward sustainable assets, while a common theoretical view is that the benefits of ESG investing should be offset by lower expected returns as investors bid up the prices of assets with better ESG characteristics.9 To address this question, we extend the conceptual framework of Berk and Green (2004) to an ESG setting in which fund investors derive utility from both benchmark-adjusted returns (i.e., alpha) and non-pecuniary benefits from ESG investing (i.e., ESG performance). Funds face decreasing returns to scale in active portfolio management, and investors supply capital until the total value added from net-of-fees alpha and ESG performance is expected to be zero. The framework delivers two predictions. First, funds with higher alpha and ESG performance have higher future flows, consistent with our empirical evidence discussed above. Second, a fund’s value added from alpha—net-of-fees benchmark-adjusted returns multiplied by AUM—represents the shadow price of ESG performance, or equivalently the negative of ESG value added. In other words, a fund’s ESG performance is negatively associated with its financial value added and, hence, fund investors face an ESG–return trade-off.To test this prediction, we first compare the realized benchmark-adjusted returns of funds in the top decile of FlowESĜ with those in the bottom decile. The annualized average return spread over the subsequent 36 months is −0.72% (t-statistic =−2.48). The negative return predictability of FlowESĜ remains economically and statistically significant after controlling for fund characteristics, including fund size, expense ratio, turnover ratio, CAPM α, Morningstar Star Rating, and fund R2, a well-known predictor of fund performance (Amihud and Goyenko, 2013). Following the approach in Berk and Van Binsbergen (2015), we then compute funds’ value added and find that funds in the top decile of ESG performance deliver $48 million per year more ESG value added than funds in the bottom decile. Based on ex post realized fund returns, our findings suggest that mutual fund investors face an ESG–return tradeoff: funds with better ESG performance deliver significantly less value added from alpha.We also address the concern that ESG premia and value added may be estimated imprecisely because the time series of realized returns are short and noisy. At the stock level, prior studies address this issue by computing forward-looking, ex ante measures of expected returns (e.g., Pástor et al., 2022, Eskildsen et al., 2024). We apply this approach in the mutual fund setting to construct four ex ante measures of expected benchmark-adjusted fund returns and value added. These measures are based on alternative estimates of the expected returns of the stocks held by each fund and its benchmark index. Consistent with our results using ex post realized fund returns, high-FlowESĜ funds deliver lower expected benchmark-adjusted returns and higher expected ESG value added. In addition, the estimated ex ante return spreads have smaller standard errors and range from −0.38% to −2.34%, depending on the measure.Taken together, our evidence shows that investors respond positively to funds with better ESG performance (i.e., higher FlowESĜ), despite holding ex ante beliefs that such funds deliver poor financial performance. Hence, investors’ positive flow response to FlowESĜ likely reflects ESG preferences rather than the belief that a fund’s ESG tilts signal higher future returns. To further disentangle preferences from beliefs, we examine outflows (redemptions) from funds with better ESG performance when those funds perform poorly in returns (i.e., have a Morningstar Star Rating of one). Interestingly, we find that investors redeem less capital from such funds. This pattern is consistent with strong ESG preferences: investors continue to invest sustainably even when such funds perform poorly.Our main findings survive many variations of the baseline analysis. First, the predictive power of FlowESĜ is not materially altered by including FlowFundChar̂ and FlowPortChar̂—ML flow forecasts based on large sets of fund characteristics and portfolio characteristics constructed from firm financial ratios other than ESG scores. Second, our portfolio-sort results are qualitatively similar when using equally weighted portfolios instead of value-weighted portfolios, but the estimated dollar amount investors are willing to pay for a top ESG fund is smaller ($21 versus $48 million per year). Third, FlowESĜ remains predictive of future fund flows when it is constructed using alternative ML models—Elastic Net, Random Forest, and Convolutional Neural Networks—instead of BRT. Fourth, our qualitative results are unchanged when we regenerate FlowESĜ after excluding all scores from any given ESG rating agency, alleviating concerns that our findings are driven by any specific agency’s data. Finally, FlowESĜ has no predictive power in a placebo test in which it is generated by training on randomly reshuffled ESG scores, making it unlikely that our results are “hard-wired” into the ML methods.Our paper contributes to recent studies of ESG investing in the mutual fund space. While Hartzmark and Sussman (2019) find that mutual fund investors react favorably to Morningstar Globe Ratings after their introduction in 2016, Gantchev et al. (2024) find that Globe Ratings do not predict flows in more recent periods. Consistent with Gantchev et al. (2024), we find that Globe Ratings fail to predict flows over 2018–2020, a period far removed from their introduction. We introduce a novel measure of a fund’s ESG performance, FlowESĜ, based on the historical relation between investor capital flows and ESG scores. In contrast to Globe Ratings, FlowESĜ robustly predicts flows throughout our sample period.We contribute to the literature that separates preferences from beliefs. Gantchev et al. (2024) argue that mutual fund investors mainly care about return performance since Globe Ratings neither predict better returns nor generate a positive flow response. In contrast, we find that investors respond favorably to funds with higher FlowESĜ despite lower ex ante expected returns. Moreover, investors in funds with higher FlowESĜ are less likely to exit after poor return performance. These patterns suggest that investors are willing to sacrifice returns for better ESG performance as measured by FlowESĜ, supporting the notion that investors are driven by ESG preferences (e.g., Riedl and Smeets, 2017).10We also contribute to recent evidence on the ESG premium. Baker et al. (2022) find that investors are willing to pay 20 basis points per year more to invest in an index fund with an ESG mandate than in one without. We focus on active equity mutual funds rather than passive funds with an ESG mandate. Using a new proxy for a fund’s ESG performance, FlowESĜ, we show that the presence of an ESG mandate does not imply better ESG performance. In addition, according to our measure, a top-ESG-performing fund delivers a 0.72% lower net alpha and $48 million per year in higher ESG value added relative to a bottom-ESG fund. This magnitude is comparable to the value added of active mutual fund managers with top stock-selection skill (Berk and Van Binsbergen, 2015).Finally, we contribute to recent evidence that ESG scores can be misleading measures of actual ESG performance.11 We introduce FlowESĜ, a novel measure that better aligns fund-level ESG performance with revealed investor preferences. We show that funds with higher ESG-driven flows have lower ex ante expected returns, consistent with a competitive model in the spirit of Berk and Green (2004) extended to fund investors with ESG preferences. In this way, we build on the findings of Van der Beck (2025) that investor ESG demand can generate significant positive price pressure in the underlying stocks.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsU.S. active equity mutual fundsOur sample of U.S. actively managed equity mutual funds spans the period from 2010 to 2020 and is constructed using data from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) Survivor-Bias-Free Mutual Fund Database, Morningstar Direct, and Thomson Reuters Mutual Fund Holdings Database.12ESG scores and mutual fund flowsIn this section, we use portfolios of individual mutual funds to examine the predictive power of ESG scores for fund flows.Machine-learning ESG-driven flowsThe results above show that relevant information is widespread across ESG issues and rating agencies. proposed.title: Machine-learning about ESG preferences: Evidence from fund flows
proposed.abstract: We construct Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) scores for U.S. active equity mutual funds using roughly 500 metrics across ESG issues and rating agencies. Under a revealed-preference framework, we use machine learning to identify issues driving fund flows and generate ESG-driven flows as proxies for ESG performance. We estimate expected benchmark-adjusted returns using ex-post realized returns and ex-ante measures. Better-ESG funds attract larger subsequent flows and face fewer redemptions after poor performance, yet have lower expected returns, indicating flows reflect investor ESG preferences rather than high-return beliefs. Investors effectively pay $48 million more annually for a top-ESG fund.

entries.title: Bankruptcy lawyers and credit recovery

source_records.title: Bankruptcy lawyers and credit recovery
source_records.abstract: I study how bankruptcy law firm advertisements affect household credit, exploiting the borders of local TV advertisement media markets. I document a significant advertising effect on filing rates and subsequently show that ad exposure is associated with better financial outcomes. I then characterize how ad-induced filers are different from existing filers in terms of case, financial, and credit variables. I find that ad-induced filers are more likely to receive a discharge, file with lawyer representation, and be first-time filers. I interpret these findings as evidence that bankruptcy law firm advertisements help mitigate frictions in the bankruptcy decision.

before.abstract_zh: 我利用地方电视广告媒体市场的边界，研究破产律师事务所广告如何影响家庭信贷。我记录了广告对申请率的显著影响，随后表明广告接触与更好的财务结果相关。接着，我刻画了广告诱导的申请者在案件、财务和信贷变量方面与现有申请者的不同之处。我发现，广告诱导的申请者更有可能获得债务免除、有律师代理进行申请，并且是首次申请者。我将这些发现解释为证据，表明破产律师事务所广告有助于缓解破产决策中的摩擦。

Bankruptcy lawyers and credit recovery☆

I study how bankruptcy law firm advertisements affect household credit, exploiting the borders of local TV advertisement media markets. I document a significant advertising effect on filing rates and subsequently show that ad exposure is associated with better financial outcomes. I then characterize how ad-induced filers are different from existing filers in terms of case, financial, and credit variables. I find that ad-induced filers are more likely to receive a discharge, file with lawyer representation, and be first-time filers. I interpret these findings as evidence that bankruptcy law firm advertisements help mitigate frictions in the bankruptcy decision.

I document a significant advertising effect on filing rates and subsequently show that ad exposure is associated with better financial outcomes. I then characterize how ad-induced filers are different from existing filers in terms of case, financial, and credit variables. I find that ad-induced filers are more likely to receive a discharge, file with lawyer representation, and be first-time filers. I interpret these findings as evidence that bankruptcy law firm advertisements help mitigate frictions in the bankruptcy decision.JEL classificationG51; K35; M37KeywordsPersonal bankruptcy; Lawyers; AdvertisingPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionPersonal bankruptcy represents the most significant debt relief option for households in financial distress.1 Despite substantial positive effects of bankruptcy on households’ labor, credit, and health (Dobbie and Song, 2015, Dobbie et al., 2017), prior work has documented the missing bankruptcies “puzzle”, an observation that the vast majority of households that could financially gain from bankruptcy do not file (White, 1998). Subsequent studies have investigated various potential barriers to bankruptcy, including liquidity constraints (Gross et al., 2014, Antill et al., 2025), and information frictions and stigma (Bernstein et al., 2022), but debates on how to reduce these barriers remain active.One key but understudied intermediary in the bankruptcy decision is the bankruptcy lawyer. Bankruptcy lawyers not only help clients navigate the filing process but also play an important role in informing the public about bankruptcy through advertising and consultations. While these lawyers have a potentially perverse financial incentive to promote filings – they are paid per case filed regardless of client outcomes – their marketing efforts may address real frictions in the bankruptcy decision.In this paper, I investigate the effect of bankruptcy law firm advertising on bankruptcy filings and household financial outcomes. I focus on local TV advertisements, which are a key channel through which bankruptcy lawyers reach potential clients. Moreover, the institutional features of local TV advertising provide plausibly exogenous variation in bankruptcy law firm ads, thus offering an ideal empirical laboratory for identifying their causal impact. Specifically, I leverage the feature of local TV advertising that requires ads to be sold at geographic media market units known as Designated Market Areas (DMAs). Following Shapiro (2018), I focus on the borders of DMAs, which generally include homogeneous counties in the outskirts of metro areas, and I argue that discontinuity in bankruptcy law firm advertisements is exogenous with respect to economic variables at these borders.I begin by estimating the causal impact of ads on bankruptcy filings. Although empirical examination has found that advertising is often ineffective (Shapiro et al., 2021), I establish that bankruptcy law firm advertising is highly effective. My estimate implies a 0.007 percentage point increase in the bankruptcy filing rate (roughly 3% of the sample median) per 1000 local TV ads per year. This effect is economically substantial; this magnitude is comparable to the effect of a $1000 rise in debt relief generosity of bankruptcy documented in Indarte (2023). This estimate is not driven by cross-state DMA borders, is robust across time and space, and is unaffected by controlling for ads by other industries.Next, I evaluate the effect of advertisements on distressed households’ financial outcomes. For this exercise, I construct a group of potential filers, i.e., individuals with high probability of bankruptcy filing based on observable credit bureau variables. Assuming that non-filers in this sample serve as the counterfactual non-bankruptcy path of ad-induced filers, this sample allows for estimating the overall effect of ads on the population most sensitive to bankruptcy. In the resulting analysis, I find that exposure to ads is broadly associated with better financial outcomes in the following years, consistent with bankruptcy being “good” for marginal filers. Ad exposure is positively associated with having a prime Equifax Risk Score,2 negatively associated with having delinquent credit, and positively associated with credit access and real consumption. To add further strength to this result, I show that employing an instrumental variable (IV) strategy using ad exposure as an instrument for bankruptcy leads to a similar conclusion, i.e., ad-induced bankruptcies are associated with better credit outcomes.To illuminate the potential mechanisms behind the positive advertising effect on financial outcomes, I then examine how ad-induced filers (i.e., “compliers”) are different from existing filers (i.e., “always-takers”). Specifically, I estimate the effect of ad exposure on the case, financial, and credit profile of the average bankruptcy filer. I find that ad exposure is associated with a higher likelihood of receiving a discharge, filing for Chapter 7, filing with lawyer representation, and being a first-time filer. Additionally, I find no evidence of ads inducing more frivolous bankruptcy cases, which I define using financial distress status and case dismissal flags.I collectively interpret these results as suggestive evidence for bankruptcy law firm ads addressing frictions in the bankruptcy decision, in particular, under-information and stigma. First, if substantial under-information and stigma existed in bankruptcy, and bankruptcy lawyers’ advertisements informed and reduced stigma, advertising would theoretically cause more filings that lead to positive financial outcomes. Second, the characterization of ad-induced filers is broadly consistent with my proposed interpretation. Specifically, filers who are ex ante under-informed and averse to bankruptcy stigma are potentially more likely to be first-time filers and successfully receive debt discharge. I argue that this proposed channel is unlikely to be dominated by an alternative channel where advertising increases lawyer over-persuasion or strategic defaults, because ad-induced filers have fewer frivolous cases and a lower likelihood of repeat filing.Finally, to further support my proposed interpretation, I leverage novel text data from publicly available client reviews of bankruptcy law firms. Using word lists acknowledging under-information or stigma, and furthermore the role of lawyers in either informing or reducing stigma, I first show a significant presence of these forces in the filer-lawyer environment. Using client ratings, I moreover show that the positive advertising effect on households’ financial outcomes is concentrated in regions with better bankruptcy law firms.This paper relates to several strands of literature. First, this paper contributes to the literature on information-based intervention in the personal bankruptcy decision. Bernstein et al. (2022) document evidence of under-information and stigma among small business owners, yet they find no long-term effect of educational videos on firm outcomes, including bankruptcy use. In contrast, peer effects can lead to bankruptcy filings via information spillovers (Fisher, 2020, Kleiner et al., 2021), but whether such bankruptcies result in better long-term financial outcomes remains unclear. I add to the literature by showing that lawyer advertising – possibly through information provision – not only causes more bankruptcies, but also that ad-induced filings lead to positive outcomes.The larger literature on the drivers of the bankruptcy decision has investigated strategic versus liquidity motives (Fay et al., 2002, Gross and Souleles, 2002, Gross et al., 2014, Mikhed and Scholnick, 2016, Indarte, 2023), peer effects (Agarwal et al., 2020, Kalda, 2020, Fisher, 2020, Kleiner et al., 2021), race and gender (Agarwal et al., 2018, Morrison et al., 2020), health insurance (Gross and Notowidigdo, 2011, Mahoney, 2015), and prior experience (Gopalan et al., 2021). Broadly speaking, this literature’s focus is limited to the filing response, leaving post-bankruptcy financial outcomes largely unaddressed. While debt relief from bankruptcy is shown to have positive effects conditional on filing (Dobbie and Song, 2015, Dobbie et al., 2017), the effect of bankruptcy filing on the marginal filer is ex ante ambiguous given that bankruptcy is not costless. This paper’s analysis is equipped with credit bureau data, which allows for estimating the effect of advertisement-induced bankruptcy using marginal non-filers, not dismissed filers, as the counterfactual.This paper also adds to the broad literature on information frictions and stigma, which are emphasized for explaining suboptimal financial decisions including sluggish mortgage refinancing (e.g., Keys et al., 2016, Agarwal et al., 2017, Andersen et al., 2020, Agarwal et al., 2023) and low take-up of social programs (e.g., Bhargava and Manoli, 2015, Finkelstein and Notowidigdo, 2019, Humphries et al., 2020, Celhay et al., 2025, Custodio et al., 2022, Gupta et al., 2023). However, it is not ex ante obvious whether information frictions in lower-stakes (e.g., tax benefits, job training) or temporary programs (e.g., Paycheck Protection Program) imply that similar issues would apply to bankruptcy, one of the most high-stakes financial decisions in an individual’s life. My findings suggest that such frictions indeed may present a significant barrier to take-up, even in a long-standing, high-impact federal program like bankruptcy.In terms of policy implications, the central takeaway from this paper is that legal advertising positively contributes to the domain of personal bankruptcy. This finding may be somewhat surprising, given the generally negative public perception of lawyers and the strict regulation of legal advertising.3 Such a skeptical prior is theoretically justifiable; when expert intermediaries – such as lawyers – are more sophisticated than their clients and face potentially misaligned fee incentives, concerns about distorted and harmful advice are legitimate. Nevertheless, my results suggest that restricting legal advertising in the context of personal bankruptcy would be counterproductive, and that advertising is possibly a key instrument for reducing barriers to bankruptcy.By documenting the effect of legal advertising in the bankruptcy context, I add to the literature on the infrastructure of personal bankruptcy, which spans policy reforms (Li et al., 2011, Albanesi and Nosal, 2018, Chakrabarti and Pattison, 2019, Gross et al., 2021, Severino et al., 2026), bankruptcy court judge leniency (Dobbie and Song, 2015, Dobbie et al., 2017, Argyle et al., 2023), credit report impact (Dobbie et al., 2020), bankruptcy trustees (Antill, 2024), and the geographic variation in these institutional features (Keys et al., 2022). My paper also speaks to the literature on advertising in consumer finance, which has found positive advertising effects on consumers (Honka et al., 2017) as well as negative effects (Gurun et al., 2016), and the literature studying financial intermediaries and experts (Greenwood and Scharfstein, 2013, Piskorski et al., 2015, Gennaioli et al., 2015, Agarwal et al., 2017, Egan et al., 2019, Robles-Garcia, 2022),4 which has primarily focused on how experts’ conflicts of interest can harm consumers. My findings suggest that bankruptcy is a domain where even conflicted advice is better than no advice (Chalmers and Reuter, 2020), and the positive gains to consumers may suggest a significant presence of demand-side constraints (Reuter and Schoar, 2024), which I propose characterizing as under-information and stigma.The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses the institutional background related to personal bankruptcy and local TV advertisements; it also describes the data used in my paper. Section 3 explains my identification strategy. Section 4 documents the effect of bankruptcy law firm ads on bankruptcy filings, and Section 5 estimates the effect of ads on credit outcomes. Section 6 characterizes how ad-induced filers are different from existing filers, and Section 7 offers an interpretation of the paper’s findings. after.title_zh: 破产律师与信贷回收
after.abstract_zh: 我利用地方电视广告媒体市场的边界，研究破产律师事务所广告如何影响家庭信贷。我记录了广告对申请率的显著影响，随后表明广告接触与更好的财务结果相关。接着，我刻画了广告诱导的申请者在案件、财务和信贷变量方面与现有申请者的不同之处。我发现，广告诱导的申请者更有可能获得债务免除、有律师代理进行申请，并且是首次申请者。我将这些发现解释为证据，表明破产律师事务所广告有助于缓解破产决策中的摩擦。

This effect is economically substantial; this magnitude is comparable to the effect of a $1000 rise in debt relief generosity of bankruptcy documented in Indarte (2023). This estimate is not driven by cross-state DMA borders, is robust across time and space, and is unaffected by controlling for ads by other industries.Next, I evaluate the effect of advertisements on distressed households’ financial outcomes. For this exercise, I construct a group of potential filers, i.e., individuals with high probability of bankruptcy filing based on observable credit bureau variables. Assuming that non-filers in this sample serve as the counterfactual non-bankruptcy path of ad-induced filers, this sample allows for estimating the overall effect of ads on the population most sensitive to bankruptcy. In the resulting analysis, I find that exposure to ads is broadly associated with better financial outcomes in the following years, consistent with bankruptcy being “good” for marginal filers. Ad exposure is positively associated with having a prime Equifax Risk Score,2 negatively associated with having delinquent credit, and positively associated with credit access and real consumption. To add further strength to this result, I show that employing an instrumental variable (IV) strategy using ad exposure as an instrument for bankruptcy leads to a similar conclusion, i.e., ad-induced bankruptcies are associated with better credit outcomes.To illuminate the potential mechanisms behind the positive advertising effect on financial outcomes, I then examine how ad-induced filers (i.e., “compliers”) are different from existing filers (i.e., “always-takers”). Specifically, I estimate the effect of ad exposure on the case, financial, and credit profile of the average bankruptcy filer. I find that ad exposure is associated with a higher likelihood of receiving a discharge, filing for Chapter 7, filing with lawyer representation, and being a first-time filer. Additionally, I find no evidence of ads inducing more frivolous bankruptcy cases, which I define using financial distress status and case dismissal flags.I collectively interpret these results as suggestive evidence for bankruptcy law firm ads addressing frictions in the bankruptcy decision, in particular, under-information and stigma. First, if substantial under-information and stigma existed in bankruptcy, and bankruptcy lawyers’ advertisements informed and reduced stigma, advertising would theoretically cause more filings that lead to positive financial outcomes. Second, the characterization of ad-induced filers is broadly consistent with my proposed interpretation. Specifically, filers who are ex ante under-informed and averse to bankruptcy stigma are potentially more likely to be first-time filers and successfully receive debt discharge. I argue that this proposed channel is unlikely to be dominated by an alternative channel where advertising increases lawyer over-persuasion or strategic defaults, because ad-induced filers have fewer frivolous cases and a lower likelihood of repeat filing.Finally, to further support my proposed interpretation, I leverage novel text data from publicly available client reviews of bankruptcy law firms. Using word lists acknowledging under-information or stigma, and furthermore the role of lawyers in either informing or reducing stigma, I first show a significant presence of these forces in the filer-lawyer environment. Using client ratings, I moreover show that the positive advertising effect on households’ financial outcomes is concentrated in regions with better bankruptcy law firms.This paper relates to several strands of literature. First, this paper contributes to the literature on information-based intervention in the personal bankruptcy decision. Bernstein et al. (2022) document evidence of under-information and stigma among small business owners, yet they find no long-term effect of educational videos on firm outcomes, including bankruptcy use. In contrast, peer effects can lead to bankruptcy filings via information spillovers (Fisher, 2020, Kleiner et al., 2021), but whether such bankruptcies result in better long-term financial outcomes remains unclear. I add to the literature by showing that lawyer advertising – possibly through information provision – not only causes more bankruptcies, but also that ad-induced filings lead to positive outcomes.The larger literature on the drivers of the bankruptcy decision has investigated strategic versus liquidity motives (Fay et al., 2002, Gross and Souleles, 2002, Gross et al., 2014, Mikhed and Scholnick, 2016, Indarte, 2023), peer effects (Agarwal et al., 2020, Kalda, 2020, Fisher, 2020, Kleiner et al., 2021), race and gender (Agarwal et al., 2018, Morrison et al., 2020), health insurance (Gross and Notowidigdo, 2011, Mahoney, 2015), and prior experience (Gopalan et al., 2021). Broadly speaking, this literature’s focus is limited to the filing response, leaving post-bankruptcy financial outcomes largely unaddressed. While debt relief from bankruptcy is shown to have positive effects conditional on filing (Dobbie and Song, 2015, Dobbie et al., 2017), the effect of bankruptcy filing on the marginal filer is ex ante ambiguous given that bankruptcy is not costless. This paper’s analysis is equipped with credit bureau data, which allows for estimating the effect of advertisement-induced bankruptcy using marginal non-filers, not dismissed filers, as the counterfactual.This paper also adds to the broad literature on information frictions and stigma, which are emphasized for explaining suboptimal financial decisions including sluggish mortgage refinancing (e.g., Keys et al., 2016, Agarwal et al., 2017, Andersen et al., 2020, Agarwal et al., 2023) and low take-up of social programs (e.g., Bhargava and Manoli, 2015, Finkelstein and Notowidigdo, 2019, Humphries et al., 2020, Celhay et al., 2025, Custodio et al., 2022, Gupta et al., 2023). However, it is not ex ante obvious whether information frictions in lower-stakes (e.g., tax benefits, job training) or temporary programs (e.g., Paycheck Protection Program) imply that similar issues would apply to bankruptcy, one of the most high-stakes financial decisions in an individual’s life. My findings suggest that such frictions indeed may present a significant barrier to take-up, even in a long-standing, high-impact federal program like bankruptcy.In terms of policy implications, the central takeaway from this paper is that legal advertising positively contributes to the domain of personal bankruptcy. This finding may be somewhat surprising, given the generally negative public perception of lawyers and the strict regulation of legal advertising.3 Such a skeptical prior is theoretically justifiable; when expert intermediaries – such as lawyers – are more sophisticated than their clients and face potentially misaligned fee incentives, concerns about distorted and harmful advice are legitimate. Nevertheless, my results suggest that restricting legal advertising in the context of personal bankruptcy would be counterproductive, and that advertising is possibly a key instrument for reducing barriers to bankruptcy.By documenting the effect of legal advertising in the bankruptcy context, I add to the literature on the infrastructure of personal bankruptcy, which spans policy reforms (Li et al., 2011, Albanesi and Nosal, 2018, Chakrabarti and Pattison, 2019, Gross et al., 2021, Severino et al., 2026), bankruptcy court judge leniency (Dobbie and Song, 2015, Dobbie et al., 2017, Argyle et al., 2023), credit report impact (Dobbie et al., 2020), bankruptcy trustees (Antill, 2024), and the geographic variation in these institutional features (Keys et al., 2022). My paper also speaks to the literature on advertising in consumer finance, which has found positive advertising effects on consumers (Honka et al., 2017) as well as negative effects (Gurun et al., 2016), and the literature studying financial intermediaries and experts (Greenwood and Scharfstein, 2013, Piskorski et al., 2015, Gennaioli et al., 2015, Agarwal et al., 2017, Egan et al., 2019, Robles-Garcia, 2022),4 which has primarily focused on how experts’ conflicts of interest can harm consumers. My findings suggest that bankruptcy is a domain where even conflicted advice is better than no advice (Chalmers and Reuter, 2020), and the positive gains to consumers may suggest a significant presence of demand-side constraints (Reuter and Schoar, 2024), which I propose characterizing as under-information and stigma.The rest of the paper is organized as follows. entries.title: Sustainable organizations

source_records.title: Sustainable organizations
source_records.abstract: We develop a theory of stakeholder governance examining how green stakeholders influence organizations. Conflicts of interest arise from heterogeneous green preferences and intensify as they diverge. Changes in green preferences can generate unexpected outcomes by shifting control rights: greener stakeholders may reduce organizational sustainability, while browner ones might enhance it. We show that a top-down approach consistently improves organizational sustainability, while a bottom-up approach can harm it. We also uncover an asymmetry in compensation and delegation decisions between green and brown principals, driven by the public good nature of social payoffs. These findings have implications for manager–employee, investor–entrepreneur, and board–CEO relationships.

before.title_zh: 可持续组织
before.abstract_zh: 我们构建了一种利益相关者治理理论，考察绿色利益相关者如何影响组织。利益冲突源于异质的绿色偏好，并随着这些偏好的分化而加剧。绿色偏好的变化可能通过转移控制权而产生意想不到的结果：更绿的利益相关者可能降低组织可持续性，而更棕的利益相关者则可能增强它。我们表明，自上而下的方法始终能改善组织可持续性，而自下而上的方法则可能损害它。我们还揭示了绿色与棕色委托人在薪酬和授权决策上的一种不对称性，这种不对称性由社会收益的公共品性质所驱动。这些发现对管理者—员工、投资者—企业家以及董事会—CEO关系具有启示意义。

While some investors, managers, and employees push for stronger environmental and social commitments from firms and other organizations, others actively oppose them, and the gap between them appears to be widening. For example, Republican-led pension funds have withdrawn mandates from ESG-focused asset managers, reallocating control over portfolio companies, while other institutional investors simultaneously demanded stronger commitments.1 Danone removed its CEO following shareholder resistance to his sustainability agenda, and Amazon has restricted worker influence following climate activism.2 Colak et al. (2024) document that CEOs facing sustainability-related conflicts are significantly more likely to be replaced. These governance conflicts share a common feature: disagreements over sustainability are resolved through reallocations of control rights. Crucially, the intensity of such conflicts is driven not by the average level of green preferences, but by the degree of polarization across stakeholders. This paper studies how heterogeneity — specifically, polarization — in stakeholders’ green preferences shapes organizational governance and, in turn, organizations’ sustainability outcomes.We develop a theory of stakeholder governance and analyze how polarization — diverging green preferences of stakeholders — affects organizations. In our model, the owner (principal) and the manager (agent) collaborate on implementing a project. The owner, who is the controlling stakeholder, can opt for either a green or brown project but incurs an implementation cost. To circumvent this cost, the owner can delegate control rights and allow the manager to select and implement the project. Control rights enable the manager to pursue their preferred project, even if it conflicts with the owner’s preferences. To mitigate this potential conflict of interest with the manager, the owner can offer an equity stake to the manager, which comes at a cost as it dilutes their own ownership.Our analysis yields two central insights about how the owner’s and manager’s green preferences affect the organization’s sustainability efforts. First, we demonstrate an asymmetry between top-down and bottom-up approaches to shaping an organization’s sustainability. Specifically, changes in the owner’s green preferences have the intended effect: stronger green preferences increase sustainability, while weaker ones reduce it. In contrast, changes in the manager’s green preferences can have unintended effects, as they may prompt the owner to reallocate control rights: a greener manager may reduce sustainability, and a browner one can enhance it. Because these effects operate through the reallocation of control rights, even small shifts in stakeholders’ green preferences can generate large changes in the organization’s sustainability. This is precisely what unfolded at Danone, where a “green” CEO’s removal by “browner” shareholders triggered a discontinuous reversal of the firm’s sustainability agenda. Second, we highlight a difference in how green and brown owners approach delegation and compensation decisions. Green owners who prefer the green project can ensure its implementation by delegating control rights while aligning incentives with the manager by offering no equity compensation. In contrast, brown owners who favor the brown project may need to provide equity compensation to align incentives if they choose to delegate control rights and may withdraw control rights if the conflict of interest with the manager becomes too severe.In our model, the asymmetry in contracts offered by green and brown owners stems from the public good nature of social payoffs. Green owners can exploit this feature to achieve perfect alignment of incentives. By offering no equity stake, they ensure that a manager always weakly prefers to implement the green project. In contrast, brown owners face a fundamental limitation—since their preferred project primarily generates monetary payoffs, a private and rival good, they cannot achieve alignment without sharing equity. To shift the manager’s preferences toward the brown project, they must share these monetary payoffs through equity compensation, creating a trade-off between the benefits of delegation and the costs of incentive alignment. Thus, our analysis reveals an asymmetry: while brown owners face the classic trade-off between delegation benefits and incentive costs, green owners can achieve their objectives by simply delegating control rights and leveraging the public good nature of social payoffs. This distinction between green and brown owners contrasts with standard principal–agent models, in which resolving conflicts of interest typically requires providing financial incentives such as equity compensation for managers (e.g., Shleifer and Vishny, 1997).Our framework challenges the conventional wisdom that ESG-linked compensation is required to effectively incentivize improvements in an organization’s sustainability. We demonstrate that such compensation — based on the organization’s social outcome — is never optimal in our framework. Green owners can align incentives without sharing ownership by leveraging the public good nature of social payoffs, while brown owners have no reason to encourage green projects through social compensation. These findings call into question common recommendations that ESG-linked compensation may be necessary to promote sustainability (e.g., Hong et al., 2016, Flammer et al., 2019), suggesting instead that such compensation may increase managerial rents without achieving owners’ objectives (e.g., Bebchuk and Tallarita, 2022). Additionally, our analysis reveals that greener managers may extract larger rents through higher equity compensation even without higher ability. This happens because brown owners must offer stronger monetary incentives to offset managers’ stronger green preferences. Our findings also challenge recent proposals advocating expanded shareholder voting rights on environmental and social issues (e.g., Hart and Zingales, 2017), as our model demonstrates that green owners may be able to achieve their desired outcomes more efficiently through delegation than through direct control.Our framework also challenges traditional perspectives on corporate sustainability and governance. Contrary to the view that managerial engagement in sustainability comes at shareholders’ expense (e.g., Friedman, 1970), our model shows that owners may rationally delegate control rights to managers, even when this leads to greater sustainability than owners prefer. This delegation occurs because it spares the owner from bearing the implementation cost, potentially making it the most efficient choice from their perspective, even though the resulting outcome is more sustainable than what the owner would have chosen directly.A natural question is whether changes in green preferences that increase sustainability also enhance welfare. We show that they need not: sustainability and welfare are distinct objectives that can move in opposite directions. We define welfare as the sum of utilities of the owner, the manager, and an outside stakeholder who captures externalities not accounted for by the organization’s decision-makers. To see why sustainability and welfare can diverge, consider a green manager who gains control rights and thereby increases the organization’s sustainability. This shift in control rights reduces welfare when society places relatively little weight on social relative to monetary payoffs. Our analysis characterizes the economic forces driving this divergence, including how shifts in control rights can simultaneously reduce sustainability and increase welfare and vice versa.Our analysis generates several additional results. First, we show that delegation and equity compensation are complements for brown owners but not for green owners. We then extend the baseline model by introducing a manager’s limited span of influence and show that this weakens a brown owner’s use of equity incentives and can increase sustainability, while leaving green owners unaffected.While we focus on owner–manager relationships, our findings apply broadly to manager–employee interactions, investor–entrepreneur relationships, board–CEO dynamics, and organizations such as NGOs and universities. Our framework rationalizes several documented empirical patterns that existing theory struggles to explain. First, Francoeur et al. (2017) find that environmentally focused firms pay lower equity-based CEO compensation, which our model explains directly: green owners reduce equity stakes to exploit the public good nature of social payoffs. Second, empirical studies find conflicting evidence on whether green investors increase sustainability (e.g., Dimson et al., 2015, Chen et al., 2020), decrease it (e.g., Kim et al., 2025), or have no effect (e.g., Heath et al., 2023). Our framework overturns the standard prediction of a monotonically positive relationship: the relationship is non-monotonic. Third, many organizations that embraced sustainability subsequently scaled back even as average public concern for the environment appears to remain high (e.g., EPIC and AP-NORC, 2025). Our framework explains these reversals as a consequence of polarization: what matters is not the average level of green preferences but the gap between stakeholders, and as this gap widens, governance conflicts intensify, and organizations may retreat from sustainability commitments. By examining control rights, we demonstrate their fundamental role in shaping how green stakeholders influence corporate sustainability. Our analysis reveals two central insights. First, we identify asymmetries between green and brown owners in their ability to align stakeholder incentives through delegation and compensation. Second, we distinguish between top-down and bottom-up approaches to sustainability, showing how they differ in their effects on governance structures and sustainability outcomes. Our findings yield novel insights into shareholder–manager conflicts, investor–entrepreneur relationships, and board–CEO interactions, generating several novel testable empirical predictions.Second, we contribute to the emerging literature on corporate polarization (e.g., Colonnelli et al., 2023, Fos et al., 2023, Kempf and Tsoutsoura, 2024, Ferreira and Nikolowa, 2025, Gormley et al., 2026) by examining how diverging stakeholder preferences affect corporate governance. (2019), both of which show that reducing profit motives shifts attention toward social payoffs. We share this economic force and extend it by formally incorporating the allocation of control rights. This generates an asymmetry between green and brown owners in their ability to align incentives through delegation and compensation. It also makes the relationship between green preferences, equity compensation, and the organization’s sustainability non-monotonic under brown ownership—equity stakes and sustainability initially rise with managerial green preferences, but are lower once control rights are withdrawn. Neither strand alone can explain how conflicts over externalities are resolved through allocations of control rights and compensation. proposed.title: Sustainable organizations
proposed.abstract: We develop a theory of stakeholder governance examining how green stakeholders influence organizations. Conflicts of interest arise from heterogeneous green preferences and intensify as they diverge. Changes in green preferences can generate unexpected outcomes by shifting control rights: greener stakeholders may reduce organizational sustainability, while browner ones might enhance it. We show that a top-down approach consistently improves organizational sustainability, while a bottom-up approach can harm it. We also uncover an asymmetry in compensation and delegation decisions between green and brown principals, driven by the public good nature of social payoffs. These findings have implications for manager–employee, investor–entrepreneur, and board–CEO relationships.
