The results have important implications for corporate decisions, portfolio management, and policymaking.KeywordsClimate risk; Regulatory risk; Corporate Bonds; Carbon emissions; Environmental policyPrevious article in this issueIntroductionInvestors and policymakers consistently raise their concerns about environmental and climate risks embedded in investor portfolios.1 Of the three primary components of climate risk (physical, technological, and regulatory), regulatory risk is the one that investors, policymakers, and others in the finance community believe has the most immediate relevance (Krüger et al., 2020, Stroebel and Wurgler, 2021), particularly because environmental regulatory costs can significantly affect firms’ operating costs and cash flows (Karpoff et al., 2005, Meng, 2017). Moreover, uncertainty about future regulation itself poses costs to firms and their investors (Pindyck, 1993, Brogaard and Detzel, 2015).2 In fact, even if a country is not currently issuing new climate change legislation, regulatory risks can still get embedded in a firm’s cost of capital through the channel of regulatory uncertainty.Researchers have examined the effects of climate and environmental risk, particularly climate regulatory risk, on asset prices, but this work has focused primarily on equity prices.3 In this paper, we argue that analyzing corporate bonds provides valuable insights into climate regulatory risk and its effects on firms’ securities more generally. This approach is important for at least three reasons. First, regulatory risk entails added uncertainty to both a firm’s equity and debt, but as pointed out by Campbell and Taksler (2003), volatility can have opposite effects on stock and bond prices. In particular, volatility can increase the optionality of a company’s equity, adding value to the stock price. At the same time it can increase the probability of default for the company’s bonds (that is, it can entail more downside risk), thus lowering the bond price. These relationships imply that increases in climate regulatory risk can have mixed effects on equity prices, but more straightforward effects on bond prices. Thus, it is important to understand the effects on debt instruments as they may be even greater due to the downside risk inherent in such securities. Second, by studying how a firm’s bond and equity prices respond to changes in climate regulatory risk, we can employ a structural credit model to tease out the impact from asset value shocks versus volatility shocks. This is a contribution to the literature where extant studies typically examine the asset pricing effect of climate and environmental risk on a single asset class. Finally, as pointed out by Gourio (2013), for many corporations, the bond market, rather than the equity market, is the marginal source of finance.In considering the effects of regulatory risks on corporate bond ratings and pricing, we also examine whether the effects are compounded when firms’ operations are located in places with more stringent regulatory enforcement. In the United States, significant environmental legislation exists at the federal level with implementation arising from rulemaking by the EPA. However, state governments generally hold the primary responsibility for enforcing these laws, and the states vary widely in their enforcement practices, with some states imposing additional environmental restrictions beyond those required by the EPA.4 Consequently, we estimate a firm’s regulatory risk exposure by aggregating measures of the regulatory stringency a firm faces given the geographical locations of the firm’s establishments. Thus, even when two firms have objectively similar levels of environmental impact, depending on the local regulatory conditions at their facility locations, the regulatory risks they face can differ.In initial analyses, we use a sample of newly-issued corporate bonds to examine whether bond credit ratings and yield spreads are associated with firms’ environmental profiles, the regulatory risk exposures of their facilities, and the interaction between the two. These analyses reveal several important empirical relationships. First, we find that firms’ environmental profiles, whether measured using third-party environmental ratings or through the firms’ carbon footprints, are unconditionally reflected in bond credit ratings and yield spreads. Firms with lower environmental scores, higher levels of carbon emissions, or higher carbon intensities (carbon emissions scaled by firm revenue) exhibit lower credit ratings and higher yield spreads, on average. These findings echo previous results in the equity market that carbon risk is priced into average stock returns and the tail risk of stocks (Bolton and Kacperczyk, 2021, Bolton and Kacperczyk, 2023, Ilhan et al., 2021). Second, and more importantly, there exists a statistically and economically significant interaction effect on credit ratings (and alternatively, yield spreads) between a firm’s environmental profile and its regulatory environment. The differences in credit ratings and yield spreads for low environmental-score firms or high-emission firms (as compared to other firms) become more pronounced when the firms operate in states with more stringent enforcement of environmental regulations. This result suggests that regulatory risk is an important channel through which firms’ environmental profiles affect their credit risks.Recognizing the potential endogenous relationship between a firm’s environmental profile and market participants’ perceptions of its risks, we consider a setting in which expectations regarding future climate regulations receive an exogenous shock, namely the December 2015 Paris Agreement, under which world governments pledged to take actions to limit future global temperature increases. When the Agreement was announced, a natural implication for rating agencies and bond investors to draw was that governments—including U.S. federal and state governments—would tighten their environmental regulations related to the mitigation of climate change.5 In fact, consistent with this presumption, at least one rating agency adjusted its baseline scenario to include expectations of increased regulations after the Paris Agreement (Moody’s, 2016). Survey results also suggest that firms upwardly revised their beliefs about future regulation intensity in their disclosure to the CDP around the time of the Agreement (Ramadorai and Zeni, 2024). The Paris Agreement shock implies that firms would face greater climate regulatory risk, especially those firms more exposed to this risk because of their business activities. The importance of this event is reflected in the fact that it is the third highest spike in the Engle et al. (2020) climate change news index.6To test the hypothesis that the Paris Agreement had greater effects on U.S. corporate bonds more exposed to climate regulatory risks, we employ difference-in-differences analyses of firms’ credit ratings and yield spreads in the months around the Agreement. The treated bonds are those issued by firms that have poor environmental scores, high carbon emissions, or high carbon intensities prior to the Agreement, or that belong to a top 15 carbon-emitting industry. Tracking bonds traded during the testing period, we find that after the Agreement, bonds from the treated firms experience an average decrease in credit ratings of 0.48 to 0.63 notch relative to bonds from other firms. These results support the hypothesis that changes in climate regulatory risk affect bond credit ratings for firms with more significant carbon footprints. Further, the results corroborate the anecdotal evidence that credit rating analysts consider expected regulatory changes when evaluating how climate risk affects firms’ default risks. In addition, we find that the yield spreads of treated bonds increase significantly after the Paris Agreement, suggesting that beyond credit rating analysts, bond investors also react to potential regulatory changes. For example, yield spreads increased by about 30 bps for bonds issued by firms with high total carbon emissions relative to bonds issued by other firms. Similarly, bonds issued by firms in a high carbon emitting industry, firms with high carbon intensities, or low environmental scores also experience a significant increase in yield spreads after the Paris Agreement.Given that the expected tightening of environmental regulations following the Paris Agreement would presumably be carried out under the state enforcement regime that currently exists, we hypothesize that any effects on credit ratings and yield spreads should be stronger for issuers operating in high-enforcement states. Consequently, we conduct a triple-difference analysis that includes an indicator variable for firms operating in states with relatively more enforcement actions. The results indicate that following the Paris Agreement, the changes in credit ratings and yield spreads for environmentally problematic firms are more pronounced for firms with establishments located in states that more strictly enforce environmental regulations.While existing literature provides evidence that the value of equities also dropped for carbon-intensive firms after the Paris Agreement, we note that the drop in equity value as found, for example, in Monasterolo and de Angelis (2020) and Mukanjari and Sterner (2023) seems small and more transitory relative to the yield spread changes we observe for corporate bonds. To jointly examine the changes in equity and bond markets, we employ a structural credit model based on Merton (1974) to analyze the drivers of the observed credit spread changes for high-carbon issuers. Our findings show that, assuming constant volatility, the observed increase in credit spreads exceeds the model-implied sensitivity of bond yields to changes in equity values (Schaefer and Strebulaev, 2008). In other words, the underlying structural parameters must change around the Paris Agreement to account for the change in both equity values and credit spreads. Consequently, we estimate the asset values and asset volatilities for bond issuers before and after the announcement of the Paris Agreement. Our results reveal a modest drop in asset values and a significant increase in asset volatilities for the high carbon firms relative to the control firms. While the high carbon firms’ decrease in asset values quickly reverses within a few months after the Paris Agreement, the increase in asset volatilities remain persistent.Based on the structural credit model, we calculate the default probabilities for the treated and control firms and observe a significant increase in the treated firms’ default probabilities of around 74 basis points shortly after the Paris Agreement, relative to control firms. The counterfactual analysis suggests that the increase in asset volatility contributes more to this change in default probability than the change in asset value. This result is consistent with the evidence in Goldsmith-Pinkham et al. (2023), which suggests that uncertainty rather than changes in asset value is the primary driver of changes in municipal bond yields. Our analyses demonstrate that climate regulatory risks can raise the probabilities that corporate bond issuers default, underscoring their potential role in generating systemic risks. Furthermore, given that critical financial institutions hold corporate bond securities on their balance sheets (Boyarchenko et al., 2021, Papoutsi et al., 2022), the results imply that climate regulatory risks can adversely affect these institutions, which could have financial stability implications.The structural model and the empirical results suggest that after the 2015 Paris Agreement, some investors would reevaluate their holdings in bonds more exposed to climate risk. Substantial theoretical and empirical research provides evidence that various segments of the institutional investor population employ differing investment strategies regarding environmental risks, including climate risks.7 Consequently, we hypothesize that after the Paris Agreement reactions should differ between the two major institutional investor types in the corporate bond market, mutual funds and insurance companies, primarily due to the variations in their typical investment horizons (Massa et al., 2013). Using difference-in-differences analyses, we find that insurance companies, which tend to have longer investment horizons, lower their holdings in the treated bonds after the Paris Agreement. In contrast, mutual funds, which tend to have shorter investment horizons, either keep their portfolio holdings in the treated bonds constant or increase their holdings.Our analyses and results contribute in a number of dimensions. First, we contribute to the literature on the pricing of firm securities with respect to climate and environmental risks and news about those risks.8 Our evidence that corporate bond investors demand higher yield spreads from issuers with poor environmental performance is consistent with earlier work on bank loans (Chava, 2014), municipal bonds (Painter, 2020, Goldsmith-Pinkham et al., 2023), and equities (Bolton and Kacperczyk, 2021, Bolton and Kacperczyk, 2023). Previous work on environmental news or environmental policy changes focuses primarily on the stock market response (e.g., Krüger, 2015, Karpoff et al., 2005, Ramelli et al., 2021), although some work examines the effects on fixed income instruments such as bank loans (e.g., Ivanov et al., 2024). Our analysis considers not only how credit rating analysts and bond investors respond to changes in perceptions of firms’ environmental regulatory risks, but also whether the responses affect firms’ asset values and asset volatilities. In addition, through our examination of firms’ exposures to EPA regulatory enforcement, we can tease out the degree to which the regulatory environment affects the risk. Thus, we are able to highlight regulatory risks as a mechanism through which climate and environmental risks and news affect security pricing.Our paper also contributes to the literature on investor preferences for environmentally friendly securities such as the work on green bonds (Zerbib, 2019, Tang and Zhang, 2020, Flammer, 2021, Baker et al., 2022a, Pastor et al., 2022, D’Amico et al., 2026), and the pricing effects of ESG on sovereign bonds (Margaretic and Pouget, 2018, Capelle-Blancard et al., 2019). We show that ratings and spreads for corporate bonds as well as their institutional investor ownership are affected by not only a firm’s environmental activities but also its regulatory risk exposures.Previous research shows the relation between firms’ costs of debt and the liability and political uncertainty risks that they face (Gormley and Matsa, 2011, Bradley et al., 2016, Kaviani et al., 2020, Ilhan et al., 2021). Our paper is particularly complementary to Ilhan et al. (2021), who examine the effects of the Trump election on firms’ tail risk by using out-of-the-money put options on firms’ equity securities. They conclude that the election was followed by significantly decreased tail risks for the top polluting industry firms. Our results not only demonstrate how policy uncertainty can increase firms’ risk, but also through a structural model we decompose the effects of the Paris Agreement into asset volatility and asset value channels. The dominance of the volatility channel over the asset value channel carries important implications for understanding how climate policy uncertainty affects financial markets. Against the backdrop of the U.S. political landscape where administrations have oscillated their stance on global climate pacts, we provide insights that the mere presence of substantial regulatory uncertainty can materially increase the cost of capital for high-emission firms in bond markets, even in the absence of concrete policy implementation.Our findings have broader implications given the corporate bond market’s significant role in the economy through its relationship with firm investment (Philippon, 2009) and potential feedback effects during market distress (Gilchrist and Zakrajšek, 2012, Gilchrist et al., 2014). Policymakers have begun monitoring corporate bond markets for financial stability reasons (Boyarchenko et al., 2021), and some central banks now purchase corporate bonds as an important policy tool. In this light, our work provides guidance for regulators in understanding the connection between climate regulatory uncertainty and the real economy through bond pricing. Further, our results are consistent with the arguments of Stiglitz et al. (2017) and Berg et al. (2023) that the uncertainty in the regulatory framework and path used by governments in the transition to combat climate change can harm the efficiency of both financial institutions and financial markets.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsSample constructionOur sample includes bonds issued by U.S. public non-financial companies, which are classified as corporate debentures and corporate medium term notes with maturities ranging from one month to 30 years.9 We obtain data on these bonds and their issuing firms over theRegression specificationsWe first examine the relationship between bond credit risks and the issuing firms’ environmental profiles, and test whether that relationship is strengthened by the firms’ exposures to differing regulatory risks across states. Towards mission theory: A systematic literature review of its critiques and avenues for progress (2010–2025)

•
Maps critiques to mission-oriented policy based on their positioning and layering
•
Reviews 224 peer-reviewed studies using PRISMA and abductive thematic analysis
•
Identifies 18 main themes split between external challenges and internal gaps
•
Reveals epistemic and analytical challenges hindering the academic debate
•
Suggests three conditions for progress within mission theory

During the last 15 years, researchers and practitioners alike showed a newfound interest in the potential of ‘mission-oriented’ innovation policy to tackle current societal challenges. In this period, the approach prompted multiple reflections and critiques from orthodox and heterodox scholars alike. However, a structured appraisal of this debate has been missing. Untangling its analytical complexity, this paper presents a systematic literature review of 224 articles and book chapters published between 2010 and 2025 to appraise the state-of-the-art debate within ‘mission theory’. Using the PRISMA Protocol and abductive thematic analysis, the paper identifies 18 themes mapped across two analytical dimensions: positioning (identifying either ‘external’ challenges or ‘internal’ gaps within mission theory); and layering (identifying challenges and gaps based on a ‘foundational’, ‘theoretical’, or ‘empirical’ ground). Building on the findings, the paper reflects on the sociological conditions preventing the progress of mission theory in contemporary research efforts – ultimately calling for greater epistemological reflexivity in the strategies adopted by researchers and practitioners to develop avenues for its further progress.

IntroductionIn the last two decades, the field of innovation policy witnessed a considerable evolution. The rise of public and scholarly emphasis on wicked problems – including climate change, inequality, health pandemics, or rapid digitalisation – prompted scholars and policy makers to reconsider the pre-extant innovation policy toolbox and reassess its conceptual landscape (Mazzucato, 2018; Haddad et al., 2022; Juhász and Lane, 2024). Against this background, the ‘mission-oriented’ approach quickly spread across the world – where the OECD identified 148 missions launched in 23 countries as of 2024 only in the innovation policy domain of ‘net-zero’ (decarbonisation) alone (OECD, 2024a). Similarly, the literature on the topic has also witnessed dramatic growth and considerable diversification over the same timeframe (OECD, 2026). Nevertheless, despite such burgeoning popularity, a proper appraisal of the diverse arguments which underlie or undermine the mission-oriented approach has been missing from the literature thus far.The mission-oriented approach has been defined by researchers and practitioners in many ways – including as “cross-sectoral and cross-policy approach” (Wittmann et al., 2021); “co-ordinated package of policy and regulatory measures” tailored to a measurable goal (Larrue, 2021); and “space for collective action to address systemic challenges” (OECD, 2024b). The thread behind such definitions is the pivotal role of missions: objectives that “translate challenges into concrete problems that require many [public, private, civic] organisations and sectors to collaborate” (Mazzucato and Dibb, 2019, p. 2). Beyond this definition, however, mission research and policy practice evolved in wildly different ways. On the side of research, missions have become an entry point for a broad set of reflections concerning the co-evolution of states and markets – including in respect to their purpose; underlying political economy; and role in shaping socio-technical transitions. On the side of practice, missions have become a ‘catch-all’ word hinting at a wide set of both old and new practices in how policy is designed and delivered – including at times through changes in governance architectures and politico-administrative cultures. Amidst of these parallel evolutions, two opposing tendencies have become increasingly apparent in the scholarly debate on mission-oriented policy.•On the one hand, the practical and fundamental value of the literature on missions has been openly questioned by a strand of volumes and publications that openly challenged its epistemic foundations; theoretical arguments; and empirical findings (Wennberg and Sandström, 2022; Henrekson, Sandström and Stenkula, 2024b).•On the other hand, the broad uptake of the mission-oriented approach resulted in a wide universe of theoretical debates, assertions, and subsequent practices which reflect both considerable conceptual ambiguity (Janssen et al., 2023) and manifold implementation challenges (Kattel and Mazzucato, 2025).Clearly, both tendencies are a critical spur for the contemporary innovation policy debate. Yet, if left unchecked, they bear risks too. The former trend (ideological contestation) may undermine the case for such a debate. The latter (conceptual fragmentation) may also lead to an excessive tribalisation of the debate into specific sub-issues too difficult to reconcile into a coherent grasp of the subject. Against this background, the assumption behind this paper is that mission-oriented policy research and practice can only advance through the joint appraisal of both its ideological contestation and its conceptual fragmentation. Bilateral exchanges have explicitly sketched out and addressed some of the main critiques of mission-oriented policy driving the academic debate – notably, between Kirchherr et al. (2023) and Hekkert (2023). Yet these exchanges remain haphazard and topic-specific. Moving beyond them requires scholars to systematise the current landscape of mission-oriented policy research into a shared epistemic architecture. In this paper, we take the critique of mission-oriented policy – i.e., any reflective examination of the validity and limits of claims inherent to this subject – as the main unit of this architecture. By doing so, we aim to reveal how different critiques interact across distinct levels of analytical abstraction, helping us sketch the evolving contours of ‘mission theory’: i.e., a shared, cumulable, and evolving corpus of knowledge on mission-oriented policy and its usage that can be subject to further scrutiny, challenge, integration, and revision.To chart the full scope of such a theory would clearly exceed the scope of any single paper. source_records.abstract: Universities face growing pressure to make clearer the public value of research, yet documented impact does not automatically translate into public recognition or legitimacy. This paper develops the concept of Communicative Responsibility, the institutional and ethical obligation to communicate research outcomes in ways that are legible, accessible, and resonant beyond specialist assessment contexts. Drawing on responsible research literatures, including Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) and Responsible Research in Business and Management (RRBM), we argue that communication should be treated as a core component of research governance and legitimacy. Empirically, we use the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) 2021 Impact Database to examine the communicative strengths and limitations of existing impact evidence. REF impact case studies are not the only way to understand research impact, nor are they primarily written for public audiences. However, they offer a useful proxy for examining how impact might be perceived and how it could be shared more effectively. Using mixed methods, we combine qualitative content analysis of 119 purposively sampled Business and Management cases with quantitative text analysis of all 504 non-redacted cases in the field. Findings show diverse impacts generated through collaboration, interdisciplinarity, and international partnerships, but also substantial variation in communicability. Cases that identify beneficiaries, pathways to change, and accessible dissemination routes are better positioned to reduce the impact-recognition gap. We contribute to theorizing Communicative Responsibility as a governance-relevant extension of responsible research. Our findings have wider implications for how universities communicate impact beyond assessment systems.

Introduction: the legitimacy challenge in research governance and the need for communicative responsibilityUniversities occupy a paradoxical position. They contribute significantly to the economy (Booth et al., 2023), civic engagement (Hassan et al., 2024), and wider societal development through research, teaching, and innovation (Johnson and Lin, 2025). Yet financial pressures, changing policy priorities, and broader societal debates have intensified scrutiny of their role and legitimacy (Duffy and Hillman, 2025). Narratives associated with privilege, cost, and rankings (Duffy and Hillman, 2025; Hazelkorn, 2015) continue to shape public perceptions, while debates around academic rigor and societal relevance question whether research sufficiently engages with real-world problems (Starkey and Madan, 2002). Even when research addresses practitioner-driven and socially grounded issues (Rodgers and Yee, 2023), its contributions often remain confined within disciplinary silos or technical frameworks, limiting visibility and resonance with policymakers, practitioners, and wider publics (Eriksson and Sundelius, 2005).In the UK and beyond, governments have responded in part through performance-based research funding systems (PRFSs) (Hicks, 2012; Reed et al., 2021). The UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) is among the most prominent examples (Hicks, 2012; Gläser and Laudel, 2016; Wilsdon, 2015), assessing outputs, impact, and environment (Research England, 2022). Such systems have institutionalized societal impact as a core dimension of research quality, encouraging collaboration beyond academia and strengthening understanding of how research contributes to economic, social, and policy outcomes (Khazragui and Hudson, 2015).A central element of the REF is the impact case study, intended to evidence the societal1 benefits of research (Research England, 2022). While these narratives are primarily produced for assessment and accountability purposes (Bandola-Gill and Smith, 2022), they nevertheless represent one of the largest and most systematic repositories of documented research impact currently available. As such, they provide a useful way to examine broader questions about how universities communicate research impact and societal value. Although not designed for public audiences (Bandola-Gill and Smith, 2022), the way impact is framed, evidenced, and narrated within these cases offers insights into the communicative practices through which universities seek to establish legitimacy and illustrate public value. This is particularly significant in a media environment characterized by polarized representations of higher education (Hazelkorn, 2015; Duffy and Hillman, 2025) and the spread of misinformation and fake news (Akeriwe et al., 2023), where narratives of inefficiency or elitism can overshadow evidence of impact (Hughes, 2021).In this paper, we use REF impact case studies as an empirical focus to explore a broader challenge: how research impact is communicated to audiences beyond academia. We argue that the communication of impact should be treated as a foundational element of research legitimacy rather than an ancillary concern. Without communicative clarity, even demonstrable impacts may fail to sustain public trust, inform decision-making, or strengthen understanding of the societal contributions of research. Building on responsible research movements including Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) (Owen et al., 2012; Stilgoe et al., 2013) and Responsible Research in Business and Management (RRBM) (Tsui, 2016; Haenlein et al., 2022), we advance the concept of Communicative Responsibility as an institutional and ethical obligation. Communicative Responsibility seeks to ensure that research outcomes remain intelligible to non-specialists, accessible beyond expert settings, and resonant across practitioner, policy, and public domains. In doing so, our work extends existing responsible research frameworks (Jirotka et al., 2017) by positioning communicability as a criterion of responsible representation.Our analysis uses a mixed-method approach drawing upon the REF 2021 Impact Database, comprising 6361 non-redacted impact cases from 157 UK universities across 34 disciplines. fields.abstract: Universities face growing pressure to make clearer the public value of research, yet documented impact does not automatically translate into public recognition or legitimacy. This paper develops the concept of Communicative Responsibility, the institutional and ethical obligation to communicate research outcomes in ways that are legible, accessible, and resonant beyond specialist assessment contexts. Drawing on responsible research literatures, including Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) and Responsible Research in Business and Management (RRBM), we argue that communication should be treated as a core component of research governance and legitimacy. Empirically, we use the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) 2021 Impact Database to examine the communicative strengths and limitations of existing impact evidence. REF impact case studies are not the only way to understand research impact, nor are they primarily written for public audiences. However, they offer a useful proxy for examining how impact might be perceived and how it could be shared more effectively. Using mixed methods, we combine qualitative content analysis of 119 purposively sampled Business and Management cases with quantitative text analysis of all 504 non-redacted cases in the field. Findings show diverse impacts generated through collaboration, interdisciplinarity, and international partnerships, but also substantial variation in communicability. Cases that identify beneficiaries, pathways to change, and accessible dissemination routes are better positioned to reduce the impact-recognition gap. We contribute to theorizing Communicative Responsibility as a governance-relevant extension of responsible research. Our findings have wider implications for how universities communicate impact beyond assessment systems.

Introduction: the legitimacy challenge in research governance and the need for communicative responsibilityUniversities occupy a paradoxical position. They contribute significantly to the economy (Booth et al., 2023), civic engagement (Hassan et al., 2024), and wider societal development through research, teaching, and innovation (Johnson and Lin, 2025). Yet financial pressures, changing policy priorities, and broader societal debates have intensified scrutiny of their role and legitimacy (Duffy and Hillman, 2025). Narratives associated with privilege, cost, and rankings (Duffy and Hillman, 2025; Hazelkorn, 2015) continue to shape public perceptions, while debates around academic rigor and societal relevance question whether research sufficiently engages with real-world problems (Starkey and Madan, 2002). Even when research addresses practitioner-driven and socially grounded issues (Rodgers and Yee, 2023), its contributions often remain confined within disciplinary silos or technical frameworks, limiting visibility and resonance with policymakers, practitioners, and wider publics (Eriksson and Sundelius, 2005).In the UK and beyond, governments have responded in part through performance-based research funding systems (PRFSs) (Hicks, 2012; Reed et al., 2021). The UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) is among the most prominent examples (Hicks, 2012; Gläser and Laudel, 2016; Wilsdon, 2015), assessing outputs, impact, and environment (Research England, 2022). Such systems have institutionalized societal impact as a core dimension of research quality, encouraging collaboration beyond academia and strengthening understanding of how research contributes to economic, social, and policy outcomes (Khazragui and Hudson, 2015).A central element of the REF is the impact case study, intended to evidence the societal1 benefits of research (Research England, 2022). While these narratives are primarily produced for assessment and accountability purposes (Bandola-Gill and Smith, 2022), they nevertheless represent one of the largest and most systematic repositories of documented research impact currently available. As such, they provide a useful way to examine broader questions about how universities communicate research impact and societal value. Although not designed for public audiences (Bandola-Gill and Smith, 2022), the way impact is framed, evidenced, and narrated within these cases offers insights into the communicative practices through which universities seek to establish legitimacy and illustrate public value. This is particularly significant in a media environment characterized by polarized representations of higher education (Hazelkorn, 2015; Duffy and Hillman, 2025) and the spread of misinformation and fake news (Akeriwe et al., 2023), where narratives of inefficiency or elitism can overshadow evidence of impact (Hughes, 2021).In this paper, we use REF impact case studies as an empirical focus to explore a broader challenge: how research impact is communicated to audiences beyond academia. We argue that the communication of impact should be treated as a foundational element of research legitimacy rather than an ancillary concern. Without communicative clarity, even demonstrable impacts may fail to sustain public trust, inform decision-making, or strengthen understanding of the societal contributions of research. Building on responsible research movements including Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) (Owen et al., 2012; Stilgoe et al., 2013) and Responsible Research in Business and Management (RRBM) (Tsui, 2016; Haenlein et al., 2022), we advance the concept of Communicative Responsibility as an institutional and ethical obligation. Communicative Responsibility seeks to ensure that research outcomes remain intelligible to non-specialists, accessible beyond expert settings, and resonant across practitioner, policy, and public domains. In doing so, our work extends existing responsible research frameworks (Jirotka et al., 2017) by positioning communicability as a criterion of responsible representation.Our analysis uses a mixed-method approach drawing upon the REF 2021 Impact Database, comprising 6361 non-redacted impact cases from 157 UK universities across 34 disciplines. source_records.title: Discounting timing strategies
source_records.abstract: A variety of timing strategies shown to generate alpha and high Sharpe ratios at the monthly horizon exhibit substantially deteriorated performance at longer investment horizons. The effect is large: multi-factor alphas are more than halved going from one-month to 10-year returns, and factors that exploit time-series predictability drive them to zero. I argue that such return dynamics reflect compensation for exposure to shocks that are particularly risky from a long-horizon investor’s perspective. I illustrate the idea by showing that seasonality in the volatility of price-of-risk and expected-cash-flow shocks generates seemingly profitable timing strategies.

before.title_zh: 折现择时策略
before.abstract_zh: 多种择时策略在月度期限上被证明能产生阿尔法和高夏普比率，但在更长的投资期限上表现显著恶化。该效应很大：从一个月到10年回报，多因子阿尔法减少超过一半，而利用时间序列可预测性的因子则使其降至零。我认为，这种回报动态反映了对冲击暴露的补偿，而从长期投资者的角度来看，这些冲击尤其具有风险。我通过表明风险价格和预期现金流冲击波动率的季节性会产生看似有利可图的择时策略，来说明这一想法。

A variety of timing strategies shown to generate alpha and high Sharpe ratios at the monthly horizon exhibit substantially deteriorated performance at longer investment horizons. The effect is large: multi-factor alphas are more than halved going from one-month to 10-year returns, and factors that exploit time-series predictability drive them to zero. I argue that such return dynamics reflect compensation for exposure to shocks that are particularly risky from a long-horizon investor’s perspective. I illustrate the idea by showing that seasonality in the volatility of price-of-risk and expected-cash-flow shocks generates seemingly profitable timing strategies.

The key insight is that shocks with varying degrees of persistence command different risk prices from long-horizon investors. I consider an investor who maximizes utility over terminal wealth.4Timing strategiesThis section briefly summarizes the 39 timing strategies that form the basis of my empirical analysis. I group the timing strategies into six thematic groups, based on their construction and provenance. The original sources and data span for each strategy are listed in Internet Appendix Table IA.1. The table also lists a short name for each grouping and strategy that I use in other tables and figures.All strategies are constructed as monthly excess returns and the strategies are rebalanced atEmpiricsIn this section I document both the single- and multi-horizon performance of the 39 timing strategies described above. The main finding is that the risk-return tradeoff of such strategies deteriorates over time and multifactor alphas drop by more than half.The results are summarized in Table 1. In Panel A, I report averages of excess returns, volatility, Sharpe ratios, alphas with respect to the Fama–French 4-factor model, and variance ratios across the 39 strategies. Here and in subsequentQuantitative modelThe motivating framework in Section 2 argues that timing strategies earn high returns because they take exposure to shocks that are risky from the perspective of long-horizon investors. In this section, I provide a quantitative illustration of the mechanism within a representative investor equilibrium model. In particular, I seek to produce a timing strategy that invests in the market portfolio only part of the time, has positive alpha with respect to the buy-and-hold portfolio, and, in keeping Timing the timing strategiesThe positive autocorrelation in returns that forms the basis of the empirics suggests an immediate improvement: the timing strategy could be timed further to invest more when recent past returns have been high, and invest less when recent past returns have been poor. Such “timed” timing strategies could be informative regarding the underlying drivers of the strategy returns. Under a mispricing view, the timed versions ought to see higher Sharpe ratios. Under fair pricing, the timed versionsConclusionThis paper documents the long-term risk-return tradeoff of a set of timing strategies. Previously documented timing strategies tend to exhibit variance ratios substantially above one and multifactor alphas that decrease with the investment horizon. Taken as a group, the 39 timing strategies have an average VR close to two at the five-year horizon, and the average five-year Fama–French 4-factor alpha is about half of the single-period average alpha. proposed.title: Discounting timing strategies
proposed.abstract: A variety of timing strategies shown to generate alpha and high Sharpe ratios at the monthly horizon exhibit substantially deteriorated performance at longer investment horizons. The effect is large: multi-factor alphas are more than halved going from one-month to 10-year returns, and factors that exploit time-series predictability drive them to zero. I argue that such return dynamics reflect compensation for exposure to shocks that are particularly risky from a long-horizon investor’s perspective. I illustrate the idea by showing that seasonality in the volatility of price-of-risk and expected-cash-flow shocks generates seemingly profitable timing strategies.

after.abstract_zh: 多种择时策略在月度期限上被证明能产生阿尔法和高夏普比率，但在更长的投资期限上表现显著恶化。该效应很大：从一个月到10年回报，多因子阿尔法减少超过一半，而利用时间序列可预测性的因子则使其降至零。我认为，这种回报动态反映了对冲击暴露的补偿，而从长期投资者的角度来看，这些冲击尤其具有风险。我通过表明风险价格和预期现金流冲击波动率的季节性会产生看似有利可图的择时策略，来说明这一想法。

decisions.title: Machine-learning about ESG preferences: Evidence from fund flows

source_records.title: Machine-learning about ESG preferences: Evidence from fund flows
source_records.abstract: We construct Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) scores for U.S. active equity mutual funds using roughly 500 metrics across ESG issues and rating agencies. Under a revealed-preference framework, we use machine learning to identify issues driving fund flows and generate ESG-driven flows as proxies for ESG performance. We estimate expected benchmark-adjusted returns using ex-post realized returns and ex-ante measures. Better-ESG funds attract larger subsequent flows and face fewer redemptions after poor performance, yet have lower expected returns, indicating flows reflect investor ESG preferences rather than high-return beliefs. Investors effectively pay $48 million more annually for a top-ESG fund.

existing_records.title: Machine-learning about ESG preferences: Evidence from fund flows
existing_records.abstract: We construct Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) scores for U.S. active equity mutual funds using roughly 500 metrics across ESG issues and rating agencies. Under a revealed-preference framework, we use machine learning to identify issues driving fund flows and generate ESG-driven flows as proxies for ESG performance. We estimate expected benchmark-adjusted returns using ex-post realized returns and ex-ante measures. Better-ESG funds attract larger subsequent flows and face fewer redemptions after poor performance, yet have lower expected returns, indicating flows reflect investor ESG preferences rather than high-return beliefs. Investors effectively pay $48 million more annually for a top-ESG fund.

Investors effectively pay $48 million more annually for a top-ESG fund.KeywordsESG; Fund flow; Value-added; Machine learningPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionAs investors allocate their savings in consideration of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors, it is important to know which ESG issues matter for investors, and how investors judge good versus bad ESG performance. Regulators, for example, need to know which ESG-related risks to highlight when proposing new disclosure rules.1 Practitioners and asset managers, meanwhile, have a business interest in understanding which ESG products are likely to be rated highly by investors.2 Accurate measures of ESG performance are also key to identifying ESG-return tradeoffs—i.e., whether products with better ESG characteristics tend to underperform in a financial sense. Yet, these questions are difficult to answer because investors’ ESG preferences are complex and likely focus on a specific few of many possible ESG issues. Indeed, Starks (2023) suggests that it does not make sense to talk about ESG issues as if they represent a consolidation of similar issues given the wide variety of designated ESG financial products.3 Furthermore, Berg et al. (2022a) find that ESG ratings services often disagree about a firm’s ESG performance. Such “ESG confusion” makes it difficult to objectively measure ESG performance even if one knew which issues were key to investors.In this paper, we use the capital flows of mutual funds to infer investors’ ESG preferences from their actions. Specifically, we relate flows to funds’ ESG scores covering a wide range of issues and rating agencies. This “revealed preference” approach identifies relevant scores based on their ability to forecast future flows.4 ESG scores plausibly contain relevant information because they are directly observed by many investors and may be correlated with latent variables that drive investor flows, such as ESG-related news events on media outlets and posts on social media about the fund or its top holdings.5 Our approach also yields accurate flow forecasts—“ESG-driven flow”—that concentrate the investor-relevant information in all scores. We propose that ESG-driven flow is a valid proxy for a fund’s ESG performance: funds with greater ESG-driven flow have ESG scores that are historically strong predictors of flows and, in this sense, align closely with investors’ preferences and have better ESG performance.Our analysis covers active equity mutual funds in the United States from 2011 to 2020. We construct a broad set of ESG scores for each fund using its stock holdings and stock-level ESG scores. These scores are based on about 500 underlying ESG metrics covering a wide range of ESG issues and six rating agencies—Sustainalytics, MSCI IVA, MSCI KLD, Refinitiv Asset4, RepRisk, and S&P Global. We categorize these metrics into a tractable number of 17 ESG issues so that, for example, all metrics related to carbon emissions and climate change are categorized into a single Climate Change & Emissions issue. In addition, we construct up to six rating agency-specific scores for each ESG issue, yielding a total of 91 scores across issues and rating agencies.6We first examine the predictive power of ESG scores for fund flows. We sort funds in month t−1 into deciles based on their scores and compute their average value-weighted flows over month t. Our first test uses a fund’s single composite ESG score obtained by averaging its 91 scores across all issues and rating agencies. Funds with scores in the top decile garner higher flows than bottom decile funds, with a flow spread of 5.36% (t-statistic =4.27).Next, we focus on scores for specific ESG issues, obtained by averaging scores across rating agencies. Many issues are associated with positive and significant flow spreads, including Waste & Pollution (E), Product Responsibility (S), and Business Ethics (G); in contrast, for other issues, the flow spreads are small and not significant. The observed heterogeneity in predictive power for investor capital flows across ESG issues supports the conjecture of Starks (2023) that, “...many, perhaps most, value and values investors do not employ the combined ESG score but rather are more interested in the individual components such as carbon footprint, animal rights, or governance quality.”We then exploit the heterogeneity in ESG scores across rating agencies. We first show that fund-level ESG scores inherit the well-known dispersion in ESG scores at the stock-level (Berg et al., 2022b). Specifically, the average pairwise correlation between rating agencies’ scores is just 0.17. The strength of the flow-ESG sensitivity is rating agency-specific for some issues but not others. For example, in case of Climate Change & Emissions, only the scores provided by Sustainalytics and RepRisk deliver positive and significant flow spreads while the Accounting & Transparency scores of nearly all rating agencies generate a significant flow response. Hence, relevant information about ESG performance is widespread across issues and rating agencies and, for some particular issues, investors respond to scores from any rating agency.To effectively capture the diverse ESG preferences driving investor capital allocation decisions, we adopt machine learning (ML) to generate accurate flow forecasts (“ESG-driven flows”) that incorporate the predictive power of all 91 ESG scores. Specifically, we use Boosted Regression Trees (BRT) as our baseline ML model to estimate the functional form relating scores available at month t−1 to flows in month t over a training and validation sample.7 We recursively train and validate BRT at each quarter-end using an expanding window of flows and scores. We then apply the trained model to generate monthly flow forecasts in the next quarter. This yields a panel of flow forecasts for each month and fund, denoted FlowESĜ, that avoids forward-looking information. By design, ESG-driven flows are higher for funds with ESG scores that are informative of future flows. In this sense, such funds align closely with investors’ ESG preferences and have better ESG performance.If FlowESĜ is a valid proxy for a fund’s ESG performance, then it should predict higher flows in the future. Indeed, we find that FlowESĜ in month t−1 predicts month-t flows outside of our training samples. Funds in the top decile of FlowESĜ realize annualized value-weighted flows of 8.86% (t-statistic =4.74) over the following month while those in the bottom decile realize −15.25% (t-statistic =−16.18). The difference, 24.11% (t-statistic =12.70), is four times larger than that from sorting on the simple composite ESG score and even more on any single score. Interestingly, the positive flows in the top decile group contrast with the overall pattern of negative flows among active equity mutual funds during the 2011–2020 period.FlowESĜ is novel because its predictive power is not subsumed by well-documented predictors of fund flows, including CAPM alpha (Barber et al., 2016), Morningstar Star Rating (Ben-David et al., 2022), and Morningstar Globe Rating (Hartzmark and Sussman, 2019). It is economically important: a one-standard-deviation increase in FlowESĜ produces 1.82% higher annualized flows, while one-standard-deviation increases in CAPM alpha and the Morningstar Star Rating are associated with higher flows of 3.00% and 2.52%, respectively. FlowESĜ also substantially outperforms simpler measures of ESG-driven flows, including those based on linear models and a narrower set of ESG scores. These empirical facts establish that combining ML with a broad set of ESG scores adds significant value in uncovering the relationship between fund flows and ESG scores.Three additional findings validate FlowESĜ as a proxy for a fund’s ESG performance. First, fund flows are more predictable when using only environmental scores (i.e., FlowÊ) following the adoption of the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, a high-profile international treaty aimed at addressing climate change. This is consistent with investors responding more favorably to better environmental performance when awareness of climate concerns is higher.8 By contrast, predictability based only on social (FlowŜ) and governance (FlowĜ) scores is not significantly altered over this period. Second, FlowESĜ performs better when it is estimated using the ESG scores of stocks in a fund’s top-dollar positions, rather than its middle- and bottom-dollar positions, consistent with investors reacting more strongly to salient information reflected in a fund’s top holdings. Third, FlowESĜ is more informative for funds with an explicit ESG mandate, suggesting that investors in such funds are more socially conscious and more sensitive to fund ESG performance.A natural and crucial question is whether FlowESĜ is also predictive of a fund’s financial performance. Asset managers often claim that they can boost portfolio returns by tilting toward sustainable assets, while a common theoretical view is that the benefits of ESG investing should be offset by lower expected returns as investors bid up the prices of assets with better ESG characteristics.9 To address this question, we extend the conceptual framework of Berk and Green (2004) to an ESG setting in which fund investors derive utility from both benchmark-adjusted returns (i.e., alpha) and non-pecuniary benefits from ESG investing (i.e., ESG performance). Funds face decreasing returns to scale in active portfolio management, and investors supply capital until the total value added from net-of-fees alpha and ESG performance is expected to be zero. The framework delivers two predictions. First, funds with higher alpha and ESG performance have higher future flows, consistent with our empirical evidence discussed above. Second, a fund’s value added from alpha—net-of-fees benchmark-adjusted returns multiplied by AUM—represents the shadow price of ESG performance, or equivalently the negative of ESG value added. In other words, a fund’s ESG performance is negatively associated with its financial value added and, hence, fund investors face an ESG–return trade-off.To test this prediction, we first compare the realized benchmark-adjusted returns of funds in the top decile of FlowESĜ with those in the bottom decile. The annualized average return spread over the subsequent 36 months is −0.72% (t-statistic =−2.48). The negative return predictability of FlowESĜ remains economically and statistically significant after controlling for fund characteristics, including fund size, expense ratio, turnover ratio, CAPM α, Morningstar Star Rating, and fund R2, a well-known predictor of fund performance (Amihud and Goyenko, 2013). Following the approach in Berk and Van Binsbergen (2015), we then compute funds’ value added and find that funds in the top decile of ESG performance deliver $48 million per year more ESG value added than funds in the bottom decile. Based on ex post realized fund returns, our findings suggest that mutual fund investors face an ESG–return tradeoff: funds with better ESG performance deliver significantly less value added from alpha.We also address the concern that ESG premia and value added may be estimated imprecisely because the time series of realized returns are short and noisy. At the stock level, prior studies address this issue by computing forward-looking, ex ante measures of expected returns (e.g., Pástor et al., 2022, Eskildsen et al., 2024). We apply this approach in the mutual fund setting to construct four ex ante measures of expected benchmark-adjusted fund returns and value added. These measures are based on alternative estimates of the expected returns of the stocks held by each fund and its benchmark index. Consistent with our results using ex post realized fund returns, high-FlowESĜ funds deliver lower expected benchmark-adjusted returns and higher expected ESG value added. In addition, the estimated ex ante return spreads have smaller standard errors and range from −0.38% to −2.34%, depending on the measure.Taken together, our evidence shows that investors respond positively to funds with better ESG performance (i.e., higher FlowESĜ), despite holding ex ante beliefs that such funds deliver poor financial performance. Hence, investors’ positive flow response to FlowESĜ likely reflects ESG preferences rather than the belief that a fund’s ESG tilts signal higher future returns. To further disentangle preferences from beliefs, we examine outflows (redemptions) from funds with better ESG performance when those funds perform poorly in returns (i.e., have a Morningstar Star Rating of one). Interestingly, we find that investors redeem less capital from such funds. This pattern is consistent with strong ESG preferences: investors continue to invest sustainably even when such funds perform poorly.Our main findings survive many variations of the baseline analysis. First, the predictive power of FlowESĜ is not materially altered by including FlowFundChar̂ and FlowPortChar̂—ML flow forecasts based on large sets of fund characteristics and portfolio characteristics constructed from firm financial ratios other than ESG scores. Second, our portfolio-sort results are qualitatively similar when using equally weighted portfolios instead of value-weighted portfolios, but the estimated dollar amount investors are willing to pay for a top ESG fund is smaller ($21 versus $48 million per year). Third, FlowESĜ remains predictive of future fund flows when it is constructed using alternative ML models—Elastic Net, Random Forest, and Convolutional Neural Networks—instead of BRT. Fourth, our qualitative results are unchanged when we regenerate FlowESĜ after excluding all scores from any given ESG rating agency, alleviating concerns that our findings are driven by any specific agency’s data. Finally, FlowESĜ has no predictive power in a placebo test in which it is generated by training on randomly reshuffled ESG scores, making it unlikely that our results are “hard-wired” into the ML methods.Our paper contributes to recent studies of ESG investing in the mutual fund space. While Hartzmark and Sussman (2019) find that mutual fund investors react favorably to Morningstar Globe Ratings after their introduction in 2016, Gantchev et al. (2024) find that Globe Ratings do not predict flows in more recent periods. Consistent with Gantchev et al. (2024), we find that Globe Ratings fail to predict flows over 2018–2020, a period far removed from their introduction. We introduce a novel measure of a fund’s ESG performance, FlowESĜ, based on the historical relation between investor capital flows and ESG scores. In contrast to Globe Ratings, FlowESĜ robustly predicts flows throughout our sample period.We contribute to the literature that separates preferences from beliefs. Gantchev et al. (2024) argue that mutual fund investors mainly care about return performance since Globe Ratings neither predict better returns nor generate a positive flow response. In contrast, we find that investors respond favorably to funds with higher FlowESĜ despite lower ex ante expected returns. Moreover, investors in funds with higher FlowESĜ are less likely to exit after poor return performance. These patterns suggest that investors are willing to sacrifice returns for better ESG performance as measured by FlowESĜ, supporting the notion that investors are driven by ESG preferences (e.g., Riedl and Smeets, 2017).10We also contribute to recent evidence on the ESG premium. Baker et al. (2022) find that investors are willing to pay 20 basis points per year more to invest in an index fund with an ESG mandate than in one without. We focus on active equity mutual funds rather than passive funds with an ESG mandate. Using a new proxy for a fund’s ESG performance, FlowESĜ, we show that the presence of an ESG mandate does not imply better ESG performance. In addition, according to our measure, a top-ESG-performing fund delivers a 0.72% lower net alpha and $48 million per year in higher ESG value added relative to a bottom-ESG fund. This magnitude is comparable to the value added of active mutual fund managers with top stock-selection skill (Berk and Van Binsbergen, 2015).Finally, we contribute to recent evidence that ESG scores can be misleading measures of actual ESG performance.11 We introduce FlowESĜ, a novel measure that better aligns fund-level ESG performance with revealed investor preferences. We show that funds with higher ESG-driven flows have lower ex ante expected returns, consistent with a competitive model in the spirit of Berk and Green (2004) extended to fund investors with ESG preferences. In this way, we build on the findings of Van der Beck (2025) that investor ESG demand can generate significant positive price pressure in the underlying stocks.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsU.S. active equity mutual fundsOur sample of U.S. actively managed equity mutual funds spans the period from 2010 to 2020 and is constructed using data from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) Survivor-Bias-Free Mutual Fund Database, Morningstar Direct, and Thomson Reuters Mutual Fund Holdings Database.12ESG scores and mutual fund flowsIn this section, we use portfolios of individual mutual funds to examine the predictive power of ESG scores for fund flows.Machine-learning ESG-driven flowsThe results above show that relevant information is widespread across ESG issues and rating agencies. We now use machine learning (ML) methods to generate ESG score-based flow forecasts that utilize the information across all ESG scores.ESG-driven flow and fund performanceOur empirical results strongly show that ESG-driven flows (FlowESĜ) is a positive and significant predictor of future fund flows. We now examine the relation between FlowESĜ and a fund’s future return performance.Robustness and additional analysisWe now perform a variety of robustness tests to ascertain the strength of our main results.ConclusionMany investors emphasize Environmental, Social, or Governance (ESG) criteria to achieve certain goals. However, ESG is a complex concept and relevant information contained in commercially available ESG scores is widespread across ESG issues and rating agencies. We confront these challenges using a revealed preference approach and machine learning methods to study how the multitude of ESG scores drive the capital allocation decisions of mutual fund investors. Investors effectively pay $48 million more annually for a top-ESG fund.KeywordsESG; Fund flow; Value-added; Machine learningPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionAs investors allocate their savings in consideration of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors, it is important to know which ESG issues matter for investors, and how investors judge good versus bad ESG performance. Regulators, for example, need to know which ESG-related risks to highlight when proposing new disclosure rules.1 Practitioners and asset managers, meanwhile, have a business interest in understanding which ESG products are likely to be rated highly by investors.2 Accurate measures of ESG performance are also key to identifying ESG-return tradeoffs—i.e., whether products with better ESG characteristics tend to underperform in a financial sense. Yet, these questions are difficult to answer because investors’ ESG preferences are complex and likely focus on a specific few of many possible ESG issues. Indeed, Starks (2023) suggests that it does not make sense to talk about ESG issues as if they represent a consolidation of similar issues given the wide variety of designated ESG financial products.3 Furthermore, Berg et al. (2022a) find that ESG ratings services often disagree about a firm’s ESG performance. Such “ESG confusion” makes it difficult to objectively measure ESG performance even if one knew which issues were key to investors.In this paper, we use the capital flows of mutual funds to infer investors’ ESG preferences from their actions. Specifically, we relate flows to funds’ ESG scores covering a wide range of issues and rating agencies. This “revealed preference” approach identifies relevant scores based on their ability to forecast future flows.4 ESG scores plausibly contain relevant information because they are directly observed by many investors and may be correlated with latent variables that drive investor flows, such as ESG-related news events on media outlets and posts on social media about the fund or its top holdings.5 Our approach also yields accurate flow forecasts—“ESG-driven flow”—that concentrate the investor-relevant information in all scores. We propose that ESG-driven flow is a valid proxy for a fund’s ESG performance: funds with greater ESG-driven flow have ESG scores that are historically strong predictors of flows and, in this sense, align closely with investors’ preferences and have better ESG performance.Our analysis covers active equity mutual funds in the United States from 2011 to 2020. We construct a broad set of ESG scores for each fund using its stock holdings and stock-level ESG scores. These scores are based on about 500 underlying ESG metrics covering a wide range of ESG issues and six rating agencies—Sustainalytics, MSCI IVA, MSCI KLD, Refinitiv Asset4, RepRisk, and S&P Global. We categorize these metrics into a tractable number of 17 ESG issues so that, for example, all metrics related to carbon emissions and climate change are categorized into a single Climate Change & Emissions issue. In addition, we construct up to six rating agency-specific scores for each ESG issue, yielding a total of 91 scores across issues and rating agencies.6We first examine the predictive power of ESG scores for fund flows. We sort funds in month t−1 into deciles based on their scores and compute their average value-weighted flows over month t. Our first test uses a fund’s single composite ESG score obtained by averaging its 91 scores across all issues and rating agencies. Funds with scores in the top decile garner higher flows than bottom decile funds, with a flow spread of 5.36% (t-statistic =4.27).Next, we focus on scores for specific ESG issues, obtained by averaging scores across rating agencies. Many issues are associated with positive and significant flow spreads, including Waste & Pollution (E), Product Responsibility (S), and Business Ethics (G); in contrast, for other issues, the flow spreads are small and not significant. The observed heterogeneity in predictive power for investor capital flows across ESG issues supports the conjecture of Starks (2023) that, “...many, perhaps most, value and values investors do not employ the combined ESG score but rather are more interested in the individual components such as carbon footprint, animal rights, or governance quality.”We then exploit the heterogeneity in ESG scores across rating agencies. We first show that fund-level ESG scores inherit the well-known dispersion in ESG scores at the stock-level (Berg et al., 2022b). Specifically, the average pairwise correlation between rating agencies’ scores is just 0.17. The strength of the flow-ESG sensitivity is rating agency-specific for some issues but not others. For example, in case of Climate Change & Emissions, only the scores provided by Sustainalytics and RepRisk deliver positive and significant flow spreads while the Accounting & Transparency scores of nearly all rating agencies generate a significant flow response. Hence, relevant information about ESG performance is widespread across issues and rating agencies and, for some particular issues, investors respond to scores from any rating agency.To effectively capture the diverse ESG preferences driving investor capital allocation decisions, we adopt machine learning (ML) to generate accurate flow forecasts (“ESG-driven flows”) that incorporate the predictive power of all 91 ESG scores. Specifically, we use Boosted Regression Trees (BRT) as our baseline ML model to estimate the functional form relating scores available at month t−1 to flows in month t over a training and validation sample.7 We recursively train and validate BRT at each quarter-end using an expanding window of flows and scores. We then apply the trained model to generate monthly flow forecasts in the next quarter. This yields a panel of flow forecasts for each month and fund, denoted FlowESĜ, that avoids forward-looking information. By design, ESG-driven flows are higher for funds with ESG scores that are informative of future flows. In this sense, such funds align closely with investors’ ESG preferences and have better ESG performance.If FlowESĜ is a valid proxy for a fund’s ESG performance, then it should predict higher flows in the future. Indeed, we find that FlowESĜ in month t−1 predicts month-t flows outside of our training samples. Funds in the top decile of FlowESĜ realize annualized value-weighted flows of 8.86% (t-statistic =4.74) over the following month while those in the bottom decile realize −15.25% (t-statistic =−16.18). The difference, 24.11% (t-statistic =12.70), is four times larger than that from sorting on the simple composite ESG score and even more on any single score. Interestingly, the positive flows in the top decile group contrast with the overall pattern of negative flows among active equity mutual funds during the 2011–2020 period.FlowESĜ is novel because its predictive power is not subsumed by well-documented predictors of fund flows, including CAPM alpha (Barber et al., 2016), Morningstar Star Rating (Ben-David et al., 2022), and Morningstar Globe Rating (Hartzmark and Sussman, 2019). It is economically important: a one-standard-deviation increase in FlowESĜ produces 1.82% higher annualized flows, while one-standard-deviation increases in CAPM alpha and the Morningstar Star Rating are associated with higher flows of 3.00% and 2.52%, respectively. FlowESĜ also substantially outperforms simpler measures of ESG-driven flows, including those based on linear models and a narrower set of ESG scores. These empirical facts establish that combining ML with a broad set of ESG scores adds significant value in uncovering the relationship between fund flows and ESG scores.Three additional findings validate FlowESĜ as a proxy for a fund’s ESG performance. First, fund flows are more predictable when using only environmental scores (i.e., FlowÊ) following the adoption of the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, a high-profile international treaty aimed at addressing climate change. This is consistent with investors responding more favorably to better environmental performance when awareness of climate concerns is higher.8 By contrast, predictability based only on social (FlowŜ) and governance (FlowĜ) scores is not significantly altered over this period. Second, FlowESĜ performs better when it is estimated using the ESG scores of stocks in a fund’s top-dollar positions, rather than its middle- and bottom-dollar positions, consistent with investors reacting more strongly to salient information reflected in a fund’s top holdings. Third, FlowESĜ is more informative for funds with an explicit ESG mandate, suggesting that investors in such funds are more socially conscious and more sensitive to fund ESG performance.A natural and crucial question is whether FlowESĜ is also predictive of a fund’s financial performance. Asset managers often claim that they can boost portfolio returns by tilting toward sustainable assets, while a common theoretical view is that the benefits of ESG investing should be offset by lower expected returns as investors bid up the prices of assets with better ESG characteristics.9 To address this question, we extend the conceptual framework of Berk and Green (2004) to an ESG setting in which fund investors derive utility from both benchmark-adjusted returns (i.e., alpha) and non-pecuniary benefits from ESG investing (i.e., ESG performance). Funds face decreasing returns to scale in active portfolio management, and investors supply capital until the total value added from net-of-fees alpha and ESG performance is expected to be zero. The framework delivers two predictions. First, funds with higher alpha and ESG performance have higher future flows, consistent with our empirical evidence discussed above. Second, a fund’s value added from alpha—net-of-fees benchmark-adjusted returns multiplied by AUM—represents the shadow price of ESG performance, or equivalently the negative of ESG value added. In other words, a fund’s ESG performance is negatively associated with its financial value added and, hence, fund investors face an ESG–return trade-off.To test this prediction, we first compare the realized benchmark-adjusted returns of funds in the top decile of FlowESĜ with those in the bottom decile. The annualized average return spread over the subsequent 36 months is −0.72% (t-statistic =−2.48). The negative return predictability of FlowESĜ remains economically and statistically significant after controlling for fund characteristics, including fund size, expense ratio, turnover ratio, CAPM α, Morningstar Star Rating, and fund R2, a well-known predictor of fund performance (Amihud and Goyenko, 2013). Following the approach in Berk and Van Binsbergen (2015), we then compute funds’ value added and find that funds in the top decile of ESG performance deliver $48 million per year more ESG value added than funds in the bottom decile. Based on ex post realized fund returns, our findings suggest that mutual fund investors face an ESG–return tradeoff: funds with better ESG performance deliver significantly less value added from alpha.We also address the concern that ESG premia and value added may be estimated imprecisely because the time series of realized returns are short and noisy. At the stock level, prior studies address this issue by computing forward-looking, ex ante measures of expected returns (e.g., Pástor et al., 2022, Eskildsen et al., 2024). We apply this approach in the mutual fund setting to construct four ex ante measures of expected benchmark-adjusted fund returns and value added. These measures are based on alternative estimates of the expected returns of the stocks held by each fund and its benchmark index. Consistent with our results using ex post realized fund returns, high-FlowESĜ funds deliver lower expected benchmark-adjusted returns and higher expected ESG value added. In addition, the estimated ex ante return spreads have smaller standard errors and range from −0.38% to −2.34%, depending on the measure.Taken together, our evidence shows that investors respond positively to funds with better ESG performance (i.e., higher FlowESĜ), despite holding ex ante beliefs that such funds deliver poor financial performance. Hence, investors’ positive flow response to FlowESĜ likely reflects ESG preferences rather than the belief that a fund’s ESG tilts signal higher future returns. To further disentangle preferences from beliefs, we examine outflows (redemptions) from funds with better ESG performance when those funds perform poorly in returns (i.e., have a Morningstar Star Rating of one). Interestingly, we find that investors redeem less capital from such funds. This pattern is consistent with strong ESG preferences: investors continue to invest sustainably even when such funds perform poorly.Our main findings survive many variations of the baseline analysis. First, the predictive power of FlowESĜ is not materially altered by including FlowFundChar̂ and FlowPortChar̂—ML flow forecasts based on large sets of fund characteristics and portfolio characteristics constructed from firm financial ratios other than ESG scores. Second, our portfolio-sort results are qualitatively similar when using equally weighted portfolios instead of value-weighted portfolios, but the estimated dollar amount investors are willing to pay for a top ESG fund is smaller ($21 versus $48 million per year). Third, FlowESĜ remains predictive of future fund flows when it is constructed using alternative ML models—Elastic Net, Random Forest, and Convolutional Neural Networks—instead of BRT. Fourth, our qualitative results are unchanged when we regenerate FlowESĜ after excluding all scores from any given ESG rating agency, alleviating concerns that our findings are driven by any specific agency’s data. Finally, FlowESĜ has no predictive power in a placebo test in which it is generated by training on randomly reshuffled ESG scores, making it unlikely that our results are “hard-wired” into the ML methods.Our paper contributes to recent studies of ESG investing in the mutual fund space. While Hartzmark and Sussman (2019) find that mutual fund investors react favorably to Morningstar Globe Ratings after their introduction in 2016, Gantchev et al. (2024) find that Globe Ratings do not predict flows in more recent periods. Consistent with Gantchev et al. (2024), we find that Globe Ratings fail to predict flows over 2018–2020, a period far removed from their introduction. We introduce a novel measure of a fund’s ESG performance, FlowESĜ, based on the historical relation between investor capital flows and ESG scores. In contrast to Globe Ratings, FlowESĜ robustly predicts flows throughout our sample period.We contribute to the literature that separates preferences from beliefs. Gantchev et al. (2024) argue that mutual fund investors mainly care about return performance since Globe Ratings neither predict better returns nor generate a positive flow response. In contrast, we find that investors respond favorably to funds with higher FlowESĜ despite lower ex ante expected returns. Moreover, investors in funds with higher FlowESĜ are less likely to exit after poor return performance. These patterns suggest that investors are willing to sacrifice returns for better ESG performance as measured by FlowESĜ, supporting the notion that investors are driven by ESG preferences (e.g., Riedl and Smeets, 2017).10We also contribute to recent evidence on the ESG premium. Baker et al. (2022) find that investors are willing to pay 20 basis points per year more to invest in an index fund with an ESG mandate than in one without. We focus on active equity mutual funds rather than passive funds with an ESG mandate. Using a new proxy for a fund’s ESG performance, FlowESĜ, we show that the presence of an ESG mandate does not imply better ESG performance. In addition, according to our measure, a top-ESG-performing fund delivers a 0.72% lower net alpha and $48 million per year in higher ESG value added relative to a bottom-ESG fund. This magnitude is comparable to the value added of active mutual fund managers with top stock-selection skill (Berk and Van Binsbergen, 2015).Finally, we contribute to recent evidence that ESG scores can be misleading measures of actual ESG performance.11 We introduce FlowESĜ, a novel measure that better aligns fund-level ESG performance with revealed investor preferences. We show that funds with higher ESG-driven flows have lower ex ante expected returns, consistent with a competitive model in the spirit of Berk and Green (2004) extended to fund investors with ESG preferences. In this way, we build on the findings of Van der Beck (2025) that investor ESG demand can generate significant positive price pressure in the underlying stocks.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsU.S. active equity mutual fundsOur sample of U.S. actively managed equity mutual funds spans the period from 2010 to 2020 and is constructed using data from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) Survivor-Bias-Free Mutual Fund Database, Morningstar Direct, and Thomson Reuters Mutual Fund Holdings Database.12ESG scores and mutual fund flowsIn this section, we use portfolios of individual mutual funds to examine the predictive power of ESG scores for fund flows.Machine-learning ESG-driven flowsThe results above show that relevant information is widespread across ESG issues and rating agencies. We confront these challenges using a revealed preference approach and machine learning methods to study how the multitude of ESG scores drive the capital allocation decisions of mutual fund investors.
